sections.heading: Statement
sections.text:
Let $F$ be a field and $q\in F^{\times}$ with quantum characteristic $e$ ([[def-quantum-characteristic-of-an-invertible-hecke-parameter]]), and let $S^{\lambda}$ be the type-A Hecke Specht module of this page in the Dipper-James convention ([[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]]) for $\lambda\vdash n$. Then for all partitions $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$ the modules $S^{\lambda}$ and $S^{\mu}$ lie in the same block of $H_{F,q}(S_n)$ if and only if $\lambda$ and $\mu$ have the same $e$-core ([[def-e-core-e-quotient-and-e-weight]]). Equivalently the blocks of $H_{F,q}(S_n)$ are indexed by the $e$-cores $\gamma$ of size at most $n$ with $|\gamma|\equiv n\pmod e$, and the block of $S^{\lambda}$ is determined by $C_e(\lambda)$. (For $e=\infty$ the Hecke algebra is semisimple and each partition is its own core, so the statement is the trivial block decomposition.)

No choice principle is used.

sections.heading: Facts & Assumptions
sections.text:
**Given:** A field $F$, $q\in F^{\times}$ with quantum characteristic $e$, a partition $n\ge0$, the Hecke algebra $H=H_{F,q}(S_n)$ with Specht modules $S^{\lambda}$ for $\lambda\vdash n$, and a fixed integer $d\ge n$.

[F1] For $d\ge n$, the Schur idempotent $e\in S=S_F(d,n)$ satisfies $eSe\cong H$, and $X\mapsto Xe$ is exact. It sends each Weyl module $W^{\lambda}$ to the nonzero Murphy cell module $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$; its simple images are zero or the Murphy simple modules, with the nonzero images indexed by the $e$-restricted partitions ([[def-schur-idempotent-and-schur-functor-for-type-a-q-schur-algebras]], [[thm-schur-functor-sends-weyl-and-simple-modules-to-specht-and-hecke-simple-modules]]).

[F2] Blocks: $1=\sum_D\delta_D$ is the unique decomposition of the identity of a finite-dimensional algebra into pairwise orthogonal primitive central idempotents, blocks are the ideals cut out by the $\delta_D$, and every nonzero central idempotent is a sum of some of the $\delta_D$ ([[def-blocks-of-a-finite-dimensional-algebra-by-primitive-central-idempotents]], [[lem-the-identity-of-a-finite-dimensional-algebra-decomposes-into-primitive-central-idempotents]], [[lem-central-idempotent-decompositions-of-one-are-unique]]).

[F3] The q-Schur algebra and its Weyl modules: $S$ is finite-dimensional, $S=\mathrm{End}_H(M)$ for $M=\bigoplus_{\nu\in\Lambda(d,n)}M^{\nu}$ with $M^{(1^n)}=H$, and $W^{\lambda}_F$ has head $L^{\lambda}_F$ ([[def-type-a-q-schur-algebra-and-weyl-modules]]).

[F4] The q-Schur block theorem [[thm-q-schur-weyl-modules-are-in-the-same-block-iff-their-labels-have-the-same-e-core]]: for $\lambda,\mu\vdash n$, the Weyl modules $W^{\lambda}_F,W^{\mu}_F$ lie in the same block of $S$ if and only if $C_e(\lambda)=C_e(\mu)$; the blocks of $S$ are indexed by the $e$-cores $\gamma$ with $|\gamma|\le n$, $|\gamma|\equiv n\pmod e$; and if $e=\infty$ then $S$ is semisimple with each $W^{\lambda}_F$ its own block.

[F5] The accepted ordinary/Murphy dictionary identifies the ordinary Specht module with the fixed $\theta$ pullback of the conjugate-shape Murphy cell module. Conjugation sends $C_e(\lambda)$ to $C_e(\lambda)'$, and sends restricted labels to regular labels. In particular it preserves equality of cores. An algebra automorphism permutes primitive central idempotents and therefore preserves the same-block relation ([[def-type-a-hecke-specht-module-and-cell-form]]).

sections.heading: Proof
sections.text:
**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Central idempotents of $H$ from blocks of $S$. For a block $C$ of $S$ with primitive central idempotent $\epsilon_C$ put $\tilde\epsilon_C:=\epsilon_Ce=e\epsilon_Ce\in H$. This element is a central idempotent of $H$: it is idempotent because $\epsilon_C$ is, and for $x=ese\in H$ centrality of $\epsilon_C$ gives $x\tilde\epsilon_C=es\epsilon_Ce=e\epsilon_Cse=\tilde\epsilon_Cx$; it is nonzero because it acts as the identity on the nonzero module $W^{\lambda}_Fe=S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ for any $\lambda$ with $W^{\lambda}_F\in C$, namely $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}\tilde\epsilon_C=W^{\lambda}_Fe\epsilon_Ce=W^{\lambda}_F\epsilon_Ce=S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$. Moreover $\tilde\epsilon_C\tilde\epsilon_{C'}=e\epsilon_C\epsilon_{C'}e=0$ for $C\ne C'$ and $\sum_C\tilde\epsilon_C=e\sum_C\epsilon_Ce=e^2=1_H$. [F1, F2, F3]

1.2 Number of q-Schur blocks is at least the number of Hecke blocks. Let $H=\bigoplus_iB_i$ be the block decomposition of $H$ with block identities $b_i$. Since $M=\bigoplus_{\nu}M^{\nu}$ and $H=M^{(1^n)}$ is a direct summand, $M=\bigoplus_iMb_i$ with each $Mb_i\ne0$ (it contains $Hb_i=B_i$), and $\mathrm{Hom}_H(Mb_i,Mb_j)=0$ for $i\ne j$, because a map $f$ satisfies $f(x)=f(xb_i)=f(x)b_i\in Mb_jb_i=0$. Hence $$S=\mathrm{End}_H(M)=\bigoplus_{i,j}\mathrm{Hom}_H(Mb_i,Mb_j)=\prod_i\mathrm{End}_H(Mb_i)$$ is a product of the nonzero algebras $\mathrm{End}_H(Mb_i)$, and a product of nonzero algebras has at least one block per factor; so $\#\{\text{blocks of }S\}\ge\#\{\text{blocks of }H\}$. [F2, F3, algebra]

2.1 Number of Hecke blocks is at least the number of q-Schur blocks. Decompose each nonzero central idempotent $\tilde\epsilon_C$ of step 1.1 into primitive central idempotents of $H$ using the unique decomposition of $1_H$: every primitive central idempotent $\delta_D$ of $H$ with $\delta_D\tilde\epsilon_C=\delta_D$ belongs to exactly one $\tilde\epsilon_C$, because $\delta_D=\delta_D\cdot1_H=\sum_C\delta_D\tilde\epsilon_C$ and pairwise orthogonality of the $\delta_D$ forces $\delta_D\tilde\epsilon_C\in\{0,\delta_D\}$. Since each $\tilde\epsilon_C\ne0$ has at least one such $\delta_D$, the blocks $D$ of $H$ are partitioned into nonempty supports over the blocks $C$ of $S$, and therefore $\#\{\text{blocks of }H\}\ge\#\{\text{blocks of }S\}$. [F2, step 1.1]

3.1 A bijection of block sets, and the core criterion. By steps 2.1 and 1.2 the two block counts are equal, so each $\tilde\epsilon_C$ of step 1.1 has exactly one primitive summand and the map $C\mapsto\tilde\epsilon_C$ is a bijection from the blocks of $S$ onto the blocks of $H$. Since $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}=W^{\lambda}_Fe$ and $S^{\mu}_{\mathrm M}=W^{\mu}_Fe$, the modules $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ and $S^{\mu}_{\mathrm M}$ lie in the same Hecke block if and only if $W^{\lambda}_F$ and $W^{\mu}_F$ lie in the same q-Schur block: indeed the block of $S^{\lambda}_{\mathrm M}$ is the image under the bijection of the block of $W^{\lambda}_F$. By the block theorem [F4] the latter holds if and only if $C_e(\lambda)=C_e(\mu)$, which proves the q-Schur-normalised statement. [F1, F4, step 2.1, step 1.2]

4.1 Ordinary normalisation and semisimplicity. By [F5], $S^{\lambda}$ and $S^{\mu}$ lie in the same block exactly when $S^{\lambda'}_{\mathrm M}$ and $S^{\mu'}_{\mathrm M}$ do. Step 3.1 makes this equivalent to $C_e(\lambda')=C_e(\mu')$, and the identity $C_e(\nu')=C_e(\nu)'$ makes it equivalent to $C_e(\lambda)=C_e(\mu)$. This identity follows by conjugating every removable border strip in a core-removal sequence; the terminal core also conjugates, by independence of removal order. For $e=\infty$, $S$ is semisimple by [F4]. Its corner $eSe$ is semisimple: in the Wedderburn decomposition of $S$, each idempotent selects a subspace in each matrix factor, and its corner is a product of matrix algebras over the same division rings. Thus $H\cong eSe$ is semisimple; the block bijection separates the partition labels. This proves all assertions. [F1, F4, F5, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

cases.specific_inspection: The block comparison partitions finitely many primitive central idempotents into nonempty supports and compares their finite counts in Proof 1.2 and 2.1; it does not select elements from an arbitrary family.

sections.heading: Definition
sections.text:
Work over $\mathbb C$. Let $\lambda=(0\le p_1\le\cdots\le p_n)$ be a partition
of $N$ with transpose $q_1\ge\cdots\ge q_l\ge0$, so that $l=p_n$ is the number
of columns, and let $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{gl}_N(\mathbb C)$ with matrix units
$e_{i,j}$ in the standard basis
$v_1,\dots,v_N$ ([[def-classical-complex-matrix-lie-algebras]]). Number the
boxes of the diagram of $\lambda$ by $1,\dots,N$ down columns from the left,
and for a box $i$ write $\mathrm{row}(i),\mathrm{col}(i)$ for its row and
column, $L(i)$ for the box immediately to its left (or $\emptyset$ if absent),
and $R(i)$ for the box immediately to its right (or $\emptyset$ if absent).
Define the nilpotent endomorphism
$$e=\sum_{i:\ L(i)\ne\emptyset}e_{L(i),i}\in\mathfrak g,\qquad ev_i=v_{L(i)},$$
and declare $\deg e_{i,j}=\mathrm{col}(j)-\mathrm{col}(i)$ for all $i,j$, so
that $\mathfrak g=\bigoplus_{r\in\mathbb Z}\mathfrak g_r$ with
$\mathfrak g_r=\operatorname{span}\{e_{i,j}:\mathrm{col}(j)-\mathrm{col}(i)=r\}$.
Put
$$\mathfrak p=\bigoplus_{r\ge0}\mathfrak g_r,\qquad \mathfrak h=\mathfrak g_0,\qquad \mathfrak m=\bigoplus_{r<0}\mathfrak g_r,$$
and for rows $1\le i,j\le n$ define the shift $s_{i,j}=p_j-p_i$ if $i\le j$
and $s_{i,j}=0$ if $i\ge j$, together with the centralizer elements
$$e_{i,j;r}=\sum_{\substack{\mathrm{row}(h)=i,\ \mathrm{row}(k)=j\\ \mathrm{col}(k)-\mathrm{col}(h)=r}}e_{h,k} \qquad(s_{i,j}\le r<p_j).$$
Finally let $\chi\colon\mathfrak m\to\mathbb C$ be $\chi(x)=\operatorname{tr}(xe)$,
where the trace is the trace of the $N\times N$ matrix.

The verification below records the properties of this data that are used
throughout this page. $e\in\mathfrak g_1$ has Jordan type $\lambda$; $\mathfrak p$
is a parabolic subalgebra with Levi factor
$\mathfrak h\cong\mathfrak{gl}_{q_1}\oplus\cdots\oplus\mathfrak{gl}_{q_l}$ and
nilradical $\bigoplus_{r>0}\mathfrak g_r$, while $\mathfrak m$ is the
nilradical of the opposite parabolic; the elements $e_{i,j;r}$ with
$s_{i,j}\le r<p_j$ form a basis of the centralizer
$\mathfrak g^e=\{X\in\mathfrak g:[X,e]=0\}$; the box set
$J=\{(a,b)\in\{1,\dots,N\}^2:\mathrm{col}(a)\le\mathrm{col}(b),\ R(b)=\emptyset\}$
is in bijection with $K=\{(i,j,r):1\le i,j\le n,\ s_{i,j}\le r<p_j\}$ via
$(a,b)\mapsto(\mathrm{row}(a),\mathrm{row}(b),\mathrm{col}(b)-\mathrm{col}(a))$, and
$$\xi_{a,b}:=\sum_{t=0}^{\mathrm{col}(a)-1}e_{L^t(a),L^t(b)}=e_{\mathrm{row}(a),\mathrm{row}(b);\mathrm{col}(b)-\mathrm{col}(a)};$$
and $\chi$ is a Lie algebra character, $\chi([\mathfrak m,\mathfrak m])=0$. This
grading is the type-A pyramid good grading of the source, not the Dynkin
grading attached to an $\mathfrak{sl}_2$-triple.

sections.heading: Facts & Assumptions
sections.text:
**Given:** A partition $\lambda=(0\le p_1\le\cdots\le p_n)$ of $N$ with transpose $q_1\ge\cdots\ge q_l$, the diagram boxes with row, column, $L$ and $R$ data, the nilpotent $e=\sum e_{L(i),i}$, the grading $\deg e_{i,j}=\mathrm{col}(j)-\mathrm{col}(i)$ and the subspaces $\mathfrak p,\mathfrak h,\mathfrak m$, and the elements $e_{i,j;r}$ and $\chi$.

[F1] Matrix units satisfy $e_{h,k}e_{k,l}=e_{h,l}$ and $e_{h,k}e_{k',l}=0$ for $k\ne k'$, and the trace is $\operatorname{tr}(e_{h,k})=\delta_{hk}$ ([[def-classical-complex-matrix-lie-algebras]]).

[F2] Jordan strings: a nilpotent endomorphism is described by its strings $w,Nw,N^2w,\dots$; the Jordan type is the partition of the string lengths, and the centralizer of a nilpotent of type $\mu$ has dimension $\sum_{h,l}\min(\mu_h,\mu_l)$ ([[thm-nilpotent-jordan-string-basis]], [[def-nilpotent-endomorphism]]).

[F3] The trace form $\operatorname{tr}(XY)$ on $\mathfrak{gl}_N(\mathbb C)$ is symmetric and invariant, and the degree grading is multiplicative: if $x\in\mathfrak g_r$ and $y\in\mathfrak g_s$ then $xy\in\mathfrak g_{r+s}$, and $\operatorname{tr}(x)=0$ for $x\in\mathfrak g_r$ with $r\ne0$ ([[prop-trace-forms-are-symmetric-and-invariant]], [[def-classical-complex-matrix-lie-algebras]]).

[F4] The enveloping algebra and representations of $\mathfrak g$ ([[def-universal-enveloping-algebra]], [[def-representation-of-a-lie-algebra]]).

sections.heading: Proof
sections.text:
**Proof technique:** direct.

**Given:** The pyramid data of the Definition.

1.1 The endomorphism $e$ acts on the box basis by $ev_i=v_{L(i)}$ and $ev_i=0$ for boxes with $L(i)=\emptyset$; hence the $v_i$ in one row form a Jordan string of length $p_i$, because left shifts run from the rightmost box of the row to the first. Consequently $e$ is nilpotent of Jordan type $\lambda=(p_1,\dots,p_n)$, $e\in\mathfrak g_1$, and the number of columns is $l=p_n$. [F1, F2, F4, algebra]

1.2 Parabolic structure. The degree defines a $\mathbb Z$-grading of the associative algebra: $\deg(e_{h,k}e_{k',l})=\deg e_{h,k}+\deg e_{k',l}$ when $k=k'$ by [F1], and $[\mathfrak g_r,\mathfrak g_s]\subseteq\mathfrak g_{r+s}$. Hence $\mathfrak p=\bigoplus_{r\ge0}\mathfrak g_r$ is a subalgebra, its degree-zero part $\mathfrak h$ consists of the matrices $e_{h,k}$ with $\mathrm{col}(h)=\mathrm{col}(k)$, which is exactly the block-diagonal subalgebra with blocks of sizes $q_1,\dots,q_l$, so $\mathfrak h\cong\mathfrak{gl}_{q_1}\oplus\cdots\oplus\mathfrak{gl}_{q_l}$; the strictly positive part $\bigoplus_{r>0}\mathfrak g_r$ is a nilpotent ideal and $\mathfrak m=\bigoplus_{r<0}\mathfrak g_r$ is the nilradical of the opposite parabolic, with $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak m\oplus\mathfrak h\oplus\bigoplus_{r>0}\mathfrak g_r$. [F1, algebra]

1.3 The centralizer basis. First $[e,e_{h,k}]=e_{L(h),k}-e_{h,R(k)}$ for boxes $h,k$, with a term omitted when the relevant neighbour is absent (this is $[e,e_{h,k}]=\sum_d(e_{L(d),d}e_{h,k}-e_{h,k}e_{L(d),d})$ and $e_{L(d),d}e_{h,k}=\delta_{d,h}e_{L(d),k}$, while $e_{h,k}e_{L(d),d}=\delta_{L(d),k}e_{h,d}$ and $L(d)=k$ holds exactly for $d=R(k)$ in the same row). Now write $e_{i,j;r}=\sum_ce_{h_c,k_c}$ with $h_c$ the box of row $i$ in column $c$ and $k_c$ the box of row $j$ in column $c+r$, the sum over $c$ with $1\le c\le p_i$ and $1\le c+r\le p_j$; here $r\ge s_{i,j}\ge0$ by the defining range, so this index set is exactly $c=1,\dots,\min(p_i,p_j-r)$. Then $[e,e_{i,j;r}]=\sum_c(e_{h_{c-1},k_c}-e_{h_c,k_{c+1}})$ where a term is omitted when the neighbour does not exist; shifting the second sum by $c\mapsto c+1$ and using $R(k_c)=k_{c+1}$ (which exists exactly when $c+r<p_j$) shows that the two sums run over the same index set $\{c:c\ge2,\ c\le\min(p_i,p_j-r)\}$, because for every $c$ in the defining range one has $c+r\le p_j$; hence the commutator is $0$. The $e_{i,j;r}$ are linearly independent because they are sums over pairwise disjoint matrix units, and their number is $\sum_{i,j}\#\{r:s_{i,j}\le r<p_j\}=\sum_{i,j}(p_j-\max(0,p_j-p_i))=\sum_{i,j}\min(p_i,p_j)$, which equals $\dim\mathfrak g^e$ by [F2]. Hence they form a basis of $\mathfrak g^e$. [F2, algebra]

2.1 The bijection $J\to K$. For $(a,b)\in J$ put $i=\mathrm{row}(a)$, $j=\mathrm{row}(b)$ and $r=\mathrm{col}(b)-\mathrm{col}(a)$. Since $\mathrm{col}(a)\le\mathrm{col}(b)$ and $R(b)=\emptyset$, the column of $b$ is the full row length $p_j$, so $r<p_j$; since the box $a$ exists in row $i$ we have $\mathrm{col}(a)\le p_i$, and $\mathrm{col}(b)\le p_j$ gives $r=\mathrm{col}(b)-\mathrm{col}(a)\le p_j-\mathrm{col}(a)\ge p_j-p_i$ when $p_j\ge p_i$; hence $r\ge\max(0,p_j-p_i)=s_{i,j}$ in both cases $i\le j$ and $i>j$ (where $s_{i,j}=0$ and $r\ge0$). So the map lands in $K$, and it is injective because $\mathrm{row}(a),\mathrm{row}(b)$ determine $a$ as the box of row $i$ at column $\mathrm{col}(b)-r$ and $b$ as the rightmost box of row $j$. It is surjective: given $(i,j,r)\in K$ the rightmost box $b$ of row $j$ has $\mathrm{col}(b)=p_j$, and the box $a$ of row $i$ at column $p_j-r$ exists because $r<p_j$ and $p_j-r\ge p_j-p_i$ (for $i\le j$) or $p_j-r\ge1$ (for $i>j$), so $(a,b)\in J$ maps to $(i,j,r)$, the same index range that was established for the centralizer basis in step 1.3. [step 1.3, algebra]

2.2 The character. For $x,y\in\mathfrak m$ one has $[x,y]\in[\mathfrak m,\mathfrak m]\subseteq\mathfrak g_{\le-2}$ by step 1.2, and $e\in\mathfrak g_1$, so $[x,y]e\in\mathfrak g_{\le-1}$ and $\operatorname{tr}([x,y]e)=0$ by [F3]. Hence $\chi([\mathfrak m,\mathfrak m])=0$, that is, $\chi$ is a Lie algebra character on $\mathfrak m$: for $x,y\in\mathfrak m$, $\chi([x,y])=\operatorname{tr}([x,y]e)=0$. [F3, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 The identity $\xi_{a,b}=e_{\mathrm{row}(a),\mathrm{row}(b);\mathrm{col}(b)-\mathrm{col}(a)}$. Left shifts of $a$ run through the boxes of row $i$ in columns $\mathrm{col}(a),\mathrm{col}(a)-1,\dots,1$, and the corresponding left shifts of $b$ run through the boxes of row $j$ in columns $\mathrm{col}(b),\mathrm{col}(b)-1,\dots,\mathrm{col}(b)-\mathrm{col}(a)+1$; all these exist because $\mathrm{col}(b)-\mathrm{col}(a)+1\ge1$ and the shifts stop while the row $i$ box exists. The pairs $(\mathrm{row}(h),\mathrm{row}(k))$ obtained are exactly the pairs $(i,j)$ with column difference $\mathrm{col}(b)-\mathrm{col}(a)$ and $\mathrm{col}(h)$ ranging over $1,\dots,\mathrm{col}(a)$; by step 2.1 these are exactly the pairs indexing $e_{\mathrm{row}(a),\mathrm{row}(b);\mathrm{col}(b)-\mathrm{col}(a)}$. Hence the two finite sums coincide, and the two displayed families are the same basis of $\mathfrak g^e$. [step 1.3, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 The grading is not the Dynkin grading. If $e$ were the positive part of an $\mathfrak{sl}_2$-triple with Dynkin grading, then all degrees would be even and the degree-$1$ space would be zero for the standard normalization; here the degree-$1$ space contains the nonzero matrix units $e_{L(i),i}$, and the grading is the pyramid good grading used in the source. This convention is fixed for all finite-W-algebra constructions on this page. [step 1.1, given] ∎

sections.heading: Remarks
sections.text:
- The numbering of boxes down columns from the left makes each row a Jordan string of $e$; this is why the row lengths $p_i$ (weakly increasing) are the Jordan block sizes, while the column heights $q_j$ are the ranks' increments and index the Levi blocks of $\mathfrak h$.

- The shift $s_{i,j}=\max(0,p_j-p_i)$ counts the overlap $\min(p_i,p_j)$ of the two rows $i,j$ through the identity $\#\{r:s_{i,j}\le r<p_j\}=p_j-\max(0,p_j-p_i)$; this count is used again in the loop-mode index sets of the finite W-algebra items.

cases.specific_inspection: The pyramid Definition specifies left-shift matrix units, column degrees, the parabolic and the trace character; Proof 1.1 through 2.2 verifies these prescribed data rather than proving a criterion between two predicates.
The asserted centralizer basis and trace-character vanishing are properties of the supplied box diagram; no converse reconstructing a pyramid from an arbitrary grading or character is asserted.
There is no separate singleton criterion: a row is already a left-shift Jordan string in Proof 1.1, and the centralizer index count in Proof 1.3 is written for the given row lengths.

Box numbering, neighbours, column degrees and the trace character are explicit from the finite diagram; the centralizer verification counts finite matrix-unit sums and does not choose an infinite family.
The row and column numbers index a finite diagram rather than an interval of analytic parameters; missing left or right neighbours are handled by omission of matrix-unit terms in Proof 1.3.

sections.heading: Definition
sections.text:
Let $R$ be a commutative ring, let $n\ge0$ and $\ell\ge1$, and let $z,U_1,\dots,U_\ell$
be units of $R$ ([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]]). The **arbitrary-level
cyclotomic Hecke algebra** $H_n=H_n(R;z;U_1,\dots,U_\ell)$ is the $R$-algebra
presented by invertible commuting elements $X_1,\dots,X_n$ and generators
$T_1,\dots,T_{n-1}$ subject to the relations
$$(T_i-z)(T_i+1)=0,\qquad T_iT_{i+1}T_i=T_{i+1}T_iT_{i+1},\qquad T_iT_j=T_jT_i\quad(|i-j|>1),$$
$$T_iX_iT_i=zX_{i+1},\qquad X_jT_i=T_iX_j\quad(j\notin\{i,i+1\}),\qquad \prod_{a=1}^{\ell}(X_1-U_a)=0 .$$
For $n=0$ set $H_0=R$. The **grading variable** of this page is $v$, not the
unit $z$: the two are identified only where a statement says so explicitly.

**Multipartitions and Murphy data.** An $\ell$-**multipartition** of $n$ is an
ordered tuple $\lambda=(\lambda^{(1)},\dots,\lambda^{(\ell)})$ of partitions
with $\sum_{b}|\lambda^{(b)}|=n$ ([[def-young-tableau-standard-tableau-and-shape]]).
Multipartitions are partially ordered by dominance, $\lambda\unrhd\mu$ meaning
that $\sum_{b\le k}|\lambda^{(b)}|+\sum_{j\le m}\lambda^{(k)}_j\ge
\sum_{b\le k}|\mu^{(b)}|+\sum_{j\le m}\mu^{(k)}_j$ for all $k,m$. Fill the
diagram $t^\lambda$ with $1,\dots,n$ in component order, then row order, then
column order. Put $a_k:=\sum_{b<k}|\lambda^{(b)}|$,
$u_\lambda:=\prod_{k=1}^{\ell}\prod_{j\le a_k}(X_j-U_k)$,
$x_\lambda:=\sum_{w\in S_\lambda}T_w$, and $m_\lambda:=x_\lambda u_\lambda$,
where $S_\lambda$ is the row subgroup: the subgroup of $S_n$ stabilizing the
rows of $t^\lambda$
([[def-finite-symmetric-group-and-permutation-notation]],
[[def-generic-type-a-hecke-algebra]]). Write $M_\lambda:=m_\lambda H_n$ for
the right $H_n$-submodule generated by $m_\lambda$
([[def-left-and-right-modules]]). The **presentation involution** $*$ of $H_n$
fixes every $X_j$ and every $T_i$ and reverses products. For standard
tableaux $s,t$ of shape $\lambda$ put $m_{st}:=T_{d(s)}^{*}m_\lambda T_{d(t)}$,
where $d(s)$ is the permutation determined by $t^\lambda d(s)=s$.
Denote by $H^{>\lambda}$ the span of the higher Murphy shapes once their
basis and cell law is established by
[[thm-arbitrary-level-cyclotomic-hecke-murphy-basis-is-cellular]], and by
$S_\lambda$ the right cell (**Specht**) module with basis $m_t$ and the
action given by that cell law; its cellular form defines
$D_\lambda:=S_\lambda/\operatorname{rad}S_\lambda$, which may vanish.

**Types.** The types used below are **exactly** all $\ell$-multipartitions of
$n$, including tuples with empty components — not all multicompositions. A
**semistandard tableau** $S$ has entries the labels $(i,k)$ (row $i$ in
component $k$) ordered by component first and then by row, weakly increasing
along rows, strictly increasing down columns, and a label of component $a$
may occur only in physical component $b\le a$
([[def-semistandard-tableau-and-kostka-number]]); the **type** of $S$ is the
multipartition counting each label with the multiplicity of the corresponding
row. For standard $s$ let $\mu(s)$ be the tableau obtained from $s$ by
replacing each entry by its row-and-component in $t^{\mu}$. Put
$$m_{(S,t)}:=\sum_{s:\,\mu(s)=S}m_{st},\qquad m_{(S,T)}:=\sum_{s,t:\,\mu(s)=S,\ \nu(t)=T}m_{st}.$$
Let
$$M:=\bigoplus_{\lambda\ \text{multipartition of}\ n}M_\lambda,\qquad C_n:=\operatorname{End}_{H_n}(M),$$
with ordinary composition ([[def-direct-sum-of-a-family-of-modules]]). For
$S,T$ of shape $\lambda$ and types $\mu,\nu$, the map $\varphi_{ST}$ — once
justified by [[lem-cyclotomic-semistandard-sums-give-schur-endomorphism-basis]] —
sends $m_\alpha h$ to $\delta_{\alpha,\nu}m_{(S,T)}h$. Its right cell module
$\Delta_\lambda$ has basis $v_T$ over the semistandard $T$ of multipartition
types, with contravariant cell form and quotient $L_\lambda$. Let $T^\lambda$
be the unique tableau of shape and type $\lambda$, and let $e_\lambda$ be the
identity projection onto $M_\lambda$. Put $\omega:=(\varnothing,\dots,\varnothing,(1^n))$
and $e:=e_\omega$; then $m_\omega=1$, so $M_\omega=H_n$, and $H_n$ is an
actual direct summand of $M$. The weight projections used by the Jantzen
theory below are the $e_\nu$ with $\nu$ a multipartition. Write
$K_{(\lambda,\nu)}:=\#\operatorname{SStd}_\nu(\lambda)$ for the number of
semistandard tableaux of shape $\lambda$ and type $\nu$.

**Boundary of the definition.** All asserted module, form and map laws are
discharged by the linked local suppliers
[[thm-arbitrary-level-cyclotomic-hecke-murphy-basis-is-cellular]],
[[lem-cyclotomic-semistandard-sums-give-schur-endomorphism-basis]] and
[[thm-cyclotomic-schur-standards-and-schur-functor-control-block-linkage]];
the definition itself claims no proof of them and no primitive
residue-content classification. No choice principle is used: only finite
bases, finite subgroup and coset decompositions, finite filtrations and
explicit polynomial identities occur.

cases.specific_inspection: The Murphy datum permits arbitrary positive level and uses the same component-ordered products at level one; there is no singleton-only assertion beyond those defining conventions.
The cyclotomic presentation and the Murphy and Schur modules are definitions; their cell and map laws are explicitly assigned to the three justified_by suppliers, not to an equivalence test.
The definition constructs the multipartition-indexed endomorphism algebra and its cell modules; it does not classify all possible modules by a converse of the construction.

Repeated cyclotomic units are permitted: the presentation imposes their polynomial product without requiring distinct roots, and the Definition defers cellular module laws to local suppliers rather than assuming a semisimple specialization.
The Definition expressly sets the rank-zero cyclotomic algebra equal to the coefficient ring; the empty tuple of component diagrams and its regular summand therefore have a stated convention.

The Definition names only finite multipartition diagrams, finite row subgroups and sums of their Murphy basis entries; it explicitly states that finite bases and explicit polynomial identities use no choice principle.

The row products use initial component intervals and the flag rule permits an entry only in an earlier physical component; at the last component the remaining product is empty and the regular weight has Murphy generator equal to the unit.

Types explicitly include multipartitions with empty components, and the regular weight is the tuple of empty components followed by the column partition; this is part of the supplied Schur summand convention.

sections.heading: Definition
sections.text:
Work over the field $\mathbb C$ and fix an integer $d\ge 0$
([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]], [[def-commutative-ring]]). Let
$\mathcal F_d$ be the free associative unital $\mathbb C$-algebra on the
$d+(d-1)$ symbols $x_1,\dots,x_d,s_1,\dots,s_{d-1}$ (for $d=0$ there is only
the unit; for $d=1$ only $x_1$), with its word basis and universal property
([[lem-hh-free-associative-ring-and-relations-descent]]), and let
$I_d\mathrel{\trianglelefteq}\mathcal F_d$ be the two-sided ideal
([[def-left-right-and-two-sided-ideal]], [[def-generated-and-principal-ideals]])
generated by the following elements:

- $x_ix_j-x_jx_i$ for all $1\le i,j\le d$;
- $s_i^2-1$, $s_is_{i+1}s_i-s_{i+1}s_is_{i+1}$, and $s_is_j-s_js_i$ for
  $|i-j|>1$, for $1\le i,j\le d-1$;
- $s_ix_j-x_js_i$ for $j\notin\{i,i+1\}$, $s_ix_{i+1}-x_is_i-1$, and
  $x_{i+1}s_i-s_ix_i-1$, for $1\le i\le d-1$ and $1\le j\le d$.

The **degenerate affine Hecke algebra** is the quotient $\mathbb C$-algebra
$$H_d:=\mathcal F_d/I_d$$
with unit element written $1$ ([[thm-quotient-ring-laws]]). We keep the symbols
$x_1,\dots,x_d,s_1,\dots,s_{d-1}$ for their images, and for $w\in S_d$ we write
$w$ for the image in $H_d$ of any word in the $s_i$ representing $w$; this is
independent of the chosen word once the basis theorem below is proved. For
$a\in\mathbb C$, the notation $H_d/(x_1-a)$ means the quotient by the two-sided
ideal generated by $x_1-a$.

The verification below establishes exactly the structure of $H_d$ used
throughout this page: the ordered monomials
$$x_1^{r_1}\cdots x_d^{r_d}w,\qquad r_1,\dots,r_d\ge0,\ w\in S_d,$$
form a $\mathbb C$-basis, so that
$H_d\cong\mathbb C[x_1,\dots,x_d]\otimes_{\mathbb C}\mathbb C[S_d]$ as a vector
space with polynomial and group-algebra subalgebras
([[def-polynomial-ring-on-a-family-of-indeterminates]], [[def-group-ring]]);
$H_0=\mathbb C$ and $H_1=\mathbb C[x_1]$; for every $a$ there is a unique
algebra isomorphism
$$H_d/(x_1-a)\cong\mathbb C[S_d],\qquad x_j\longmapsto a+\sum_{k<j}(k\ j);$$
and total polynomial degree is an algebra filtration whose associated graded is
the semidirect product $\mathbb C[x_1,\dots,x_d]\rtimes\mathbb C[S_d]$ in which
$s_i$ acts by swapping $x_i$ and $x_{i+1}$. For $d\ge2$, the cross relation is
inhomogeneous, so it does not turn $H_d$ into a graded algebra with
$\deg x_i=1$ and $\deg s_i=0$. For $d=0$ the algebra $\mathbb C$ has its
degree-zero grading, and for $d=1$ the algebra $\mathbb C[x_1]$ has its
natural polynomial grading.

sections.heading: Facts & Assumptions
sections.text:
**Given:** An integer $d\ge0$, the field $\mathbb C$, the free associative $\mathbb C$-algebra $\mathcal F_d$ on the symbols $x_1,\dots,x_d,s_1,\dots,s_{d-1}$, and the two-sided ideal $I_d$ of the Definition.

[F1] $S_d$ is the group of bijections of $\{1,\dots,d\}$ under composition, with $s_i=(i\ i+1)$; it is generated by $s_1,\dots,s_{d-1}$ subject to the Coxeter relations $s_i^2=1$, $s_is_{i+1}s_i=s_{i+1}s_is_{i+1}$, $s_is_j=s_js_i$ for $|i-j|>1$ ([[def-symmetric-group]], [[def-finite-symmetric-group-and-permutation-notation]], [[thm-the-symmetric-group-has-the-coxeter-presentation]]).

[F2] $\mathbb C[S_d]$ is a unital $\mathbb C$-algebra with $\mathbb C$-basis $\{w:w\in S_d\}$, product induced by composition and unit the identity permutation ([[def-group-ring]], [[thm-group-ring-is-a-unital-algebra-with-basis-g]]).

[F3] $\mathbb C[x_1,\dots,x_d]$ is a commutative $\mathbb C$-algebra with $\mathbb C$-basis the monomials $x_1^{r_1}\cdots x_d^{r_d}$; it is a domain with fraction field $\Omega$ in which every nonzero polynomial is invertible; since $x_i\ne x_{i+1}$ as polynomials, $d_i:=x_i-x_{i+1}$ is invertible in $\Omega$ ([[def-polynomial-ring-on-a-family-of-indeterminates]], [[def-commutative-ring]], [[cor-polynomial-ring-over-a-domain-is-a-domain]], [[def-field-of-fractions]], [[thm-field-of-fractions-is-a-field-and-the-domain-embeds]]).

[F4] $\mathcal F_d$ has the word basis and universal property, the two-sided ideal generated by a set $E$ is the set of finite sums $\sum_sa_se_sb_s$ with $e_s\in E$, and a homomorphism killing $E$ factors uniquely through $\mathcal F_d/(E)$ ([[lem-hh-free-associative-ring-and-relations-descent]], [[def-left-right-and-two-sided-ideal]], [[def-generated-and-principal-ideals]], [[thm-quotient-ring-universal-property]], [[thm-quotient-ring-laws]]).

[F5] For $\mathbb C$-algebras $A,B$ the tensor product $A\otimes_{\mathbb C}B$ is a $\mathbb C$-algebra with $(a\otimes b)(a'\otimes b')=aa'\otimes bb'$; if $(a_i)$ and $(b_j)$ are bases, then $(a_i\otimes b_j)$ is a basis ([[thm-tensor-product-of-algebras-over-a-commutative-ring]], [[thm-tensor-product-basis-from-bases]]).

[F6] Algebra homomorphisms are unital ring homomorphisms over the structure map and preserve $1$ ([[def-algebra-over-a-commutative-ring]], [[def-ring-homomorphism]]).

sections.heading: Proof
sections.text:
**Proof technique:** direct.

**Given:** The data of [F1]-[F6]: the presented algebra $H_d=\mathcal F_d/I_d$, the symmetric group $S_d$, the group algebra $\mathbb C[S_d]$, the polynomial algebra $\mathbb C[x_1,\dots,x_d]$ with fraction field $\Omega$, and the tensor-product and quotient structures.

1.1 The cases $d=0,1$. For $d=0$ there are no symbols, so $\mathcal F_0=\mathbb C$ and $I_0=0$, giving $H_0=\mathbb C$. For $d=1$ the only symbol is $x_1$ and the list of relations is empty; the words in $x_1$ are $1,x_1,x_1^2,\dots$, a $\mathbb C$-basis of $\mathcal F_1$ by [F4], so $H_1$ is the polynomial algebra $\mathbb C[x_1]$ with basis $x_1^r$, $r\ge0$. [F3, F4, given]

1.2 The rational-function model. On the $\mathbb C$-vector space $\Omega$ of [F3] let $m_f$ denote multiplication by $f\in\Omega$, and for $1\le i<d$ let $\sigma_i$ be the operator $(\sigma_if)(y_1,\dots,y_d)=f(y_1,\dots,y_{i+1},y_i,\dots,y_d)$ interchanging the $i$-th and $(i+1)$-st arguments. Put $a_i:=d_i^{-1}\in\Omega$ (invertible by [F3]), $\delta_i:=a_i(1+\sigma_i)$ and $T_i:=\sigma_i-\delta_i$. For a word $w=s_{i_1}\cdots s_{i_k}$ in the generators of $S_d$ set $\sigma_w:=\sigma_{i_1}\!\circ\cdots\circ\sigma_{i_k}$ and $T_w:=T_{i_1}\!\cdots T_{i_k}$. The operators $\sigma_w$ are well defined by the Coxeter presentation [F1], because the $\sigma_i$ satisfy those relations and the presentation says that any two words for the same $w$ are related by them. [F1, F3, construct]

1.3 The skew algebra. Let $D:=\{\sum_{w\in S_d}m_{f_w}\sigma_w:f_w\in\Omega\}\subseteq\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(\Omega)$, a $\mathbb C$-subspace. For $f,g\in\Omega$ and $u,v\in S_d$ the identities $\sigma_um_g=m_{\sigma_u(g)}\sigma_u$ and $\sigma_u\sigma_v=\sigma_{uv}$ hold (the first expresses the substitution action on functions, the second is word concatenation), so $(m_f\sigma_u)(m_g\sigma_v)=m_{f\,\sigma_u(g)}\sigma_{uv}$; hence $D$ is a subalgebra of $\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(\Omega)$. The set $\{\sigma_w\}$ is $\Omega$-linearly independent: suppose $\sum_wf_w\sigma_w=0$ with $f_w\in\Omega$ not all zero; multiplying the resulting identity of functions by a common denominator of the $f_w$, we may assume $f_w\in\mathbb C[x_1,\dots,x_d]$. Fix integers $N_1>\cdots>N_d$ whose consecutive gaps exceed the total degree of every $f_w$, and order the finitely many $w$ with $f_w\ne0$ by the lexicographic order of the vectors $w\cdot N:=(N_{w^{-1}(1)},\dots,N_{w^{-1}(d)})$; let $w$ be maximal and let $e$ be the exponent of a top monomial of $f_w$. Applying the sum to the monomial $y^N$ gives $\sum_{w'}f_{w'}(y)\,y^{w'\cdot N}$, because $\sigma_{w'}y^N=y^{w'\cdot N}$; the vectors $w'\cdot N$ are distinct, and at the first coordinate where $w'\cdot N$ differs from $w\cdot N$ the gap exceeds the degree bound, so the monomial $y^{w\cdot N+e}$ occurs exactly once, in the summand $f_wy^{w\cdot N}$, with nonzero coefficient. This contradicts the vanishing of the sum, proving the claim. [F3, algebra, given]

1.4 Spanning of $H_d$ by ordered monomials. We show that every element of $H_d$ is a $\mathbb C$-linear combination of the images of ordered monomials $x^rw$; since words span $\mathcal F_d$ by [F4], it suffices to treat the image of a word $W$ in the symbols. Use strong induction on the pair $(n,\iota)$ ordered lexicographically, where $n$ is the number of $x$-symbols in $W$ and $\iota$ is the number of pairs of positions $(p<q)$ such that the $p$-th symbol is some $s_i$ and the $q$-th symbol is some $x_j$. If $n=0$, then $W$ is a word in the $s_i$; by the Coxeter presentation [F1] the subalgebra generated by the $s_i$ is spanned by the images of the elements $w\in S_d$, so the claim holds. If $n>0$ and every $x$-symbol precedes every $s$-symbol in $W$, then $W$ is of the form (word in $x$'s)(word in $s$'s), and the claim follows from commutativity of the $x$'s and the case $n=0$. Otherwise $W=W_1s_ix_jW_2$ with adjacent symbols; use $s_ix_{i+1}=x_is_i+1$ if $j=i+1$, $s_ix_i=x_{i+1}s_i-1$ if $j=i$ (the relation $x_{i+1}s_i=s_ix_i+1$ solved for $s_ix_i$), and $s_ix_j=x_js_i$ if $j\notin\{i,i+1\}$. In every case $W\equiv W_1x_{j'}s_iW_2\pm W_1W_2$, where the first word has the same $n$ and one fewer $(s,x)$-inversion pair, while the second has $n-1$ $x$-symbols; both fall under the induction hypothesis. Hence the images of ordered monomials span $H_d$. [F1, F3, F4, given, construct]

1.5 Jucys-Murphy elements. For $1\le j\le d$ put $J_j:=\sum_{k<j}(k\ j)\in\mathbb C[S_d]$, so $J_1=0$. Then (i) $J_iJ_j=J_jJ_i$ for all $i,j$; (ii) $s_iJ_j=J_js_i$ for $j\notin\{i,i+1\}$; and (iii) $s_iJ_{i+1}=J_is_i+1$. For (i) with $i<j$ write $\Omega_m:=\sum_{1\le k<l\le m}(k\ l)$ for the sum of all transpositions in $S_m$; $\Omega_m$ is central in $\mathbb C[S_m]$ because conjugation permutes the transpositions, and $J_m=\Omega_m-\Omega_{m-1}$. Since $J_i\in\mathbb C[S_i]\subseteq\mathbb C[S_{m-1}]\subset\mathbb C[S_m]$ for $i<m$, centrality of $\Omega_m$ in $\mathbb C[S_m]$ and of $\Omega_{m-1}$ in $\mathbb C[S_{m-1}]$ gives $[J_i,J_m]=[J_i,\Omega_m]-[J_i,\Omega_{m-1}]=0$. For (ii), conjugation by $s_i$ sends each transposition $(k\ j)$ to $(s_i(k)\ s_i(j))$; if $j<i$ both entries are fixed, and if $j>i+1$ the sum over $k<j$ contains the pairs with $k=i$ and $k=i+1$, whose images are interchanged, so the sum is preserved. For (iii), conjugation sends $(k\ i+1)$ to $(k\ i)$ for $k<i$ and fixes $(i\ i+1)$, so $s_iJ_{i+1}s_i=J_i+s_i$; multiplying on the right by $s_i$ and using $s_i^2=1$ gives (iii). [F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 The model satisfies the relations. Since $\sigma_im_{a_i}=m_{\sigma_i(a_i)}\sigma_i=m_{-a_i}\sigma_i$, the operator identity $(1+\sigma_i)m_{a_i}=m_{a_i}(1-\sigma_i)$ and the rules $\sigma_i\delta_i=-\delta_i$, $\delta_i\sigma_i=\delta_i$ hold; hence $\delta_i^2=m_{a_i}(1+\sigma_i)m_{a_i}(1+\sigma_i)=m_{a_i^2}(1-\sigma_i)(1+\sigma_i)=0$ and $T_i^2=\sigma_i^2-\sigma_i\delta_i-\delta_i\sigma_i+\delta_i^2=1+\delta_i-\delta_i+0=1$. For $j\notin\{i,i+1\}$ both $\sigma_i$ and $\delta_i$ commute with $m_{x_j}$, so $T_im_{x_j}=m_{x_j}T_i$. For the cross relations, use $\sigma_im_{x_{i+1}}=m_{x_i}\sigma_i$, $\sigma_im_{x_i}=m_{x_{i+1}}\sigma_i$ and the two identities $m_{x_i}\delta_i-\delta_im_{x_{i+1}}=1$ and $\delta_im_{x_i}-m_{x_{i+1}}\delta_i=1$: for the first, $m_{x_i}\delta_i=m_{a_ix_i}(1+\sigma_i)$ while $\delta_im_{x_{i+1}}=m_{a_ix_{i+1}}+m_{a_ix_i}\sigma_i$, and their difference is $m_{a_i(x_i-x_{i+1})}=1$; the second is the same computation with the roles of $x_i$ and $x_{i+1}$ interchanged. Therefore $T_im_{x_{i+1}}-m_{x_i}T_i=(m_{x_i}\sigma_i-m_{x_i}\sigma_i)+(m_{x_i}\delta_i-\delta_im_{x_{i+1}})=1$ and $m_{x_{i+1}}T_i-T_im_{x_i}=1$. Finally the braid relation: expanding $T_iT_{i+1}T_i$ and $T_{i+1}T_iT_{i+1}$ in the $\Omega$-basis $\{\sigma_w\}$ of step 1.3 by its product rule, every coefficient is a rational function of $x_i,x_{i+1},x_{i+2}$ alone whose denominator divides $d_id_{i+1}(x_i-x_{i+2})$; clearing that denominator leaves a polynomial identity in three variables, verified by expanding the six resulting permutation terms. Hence the assignment $x_i\mapsto m_{x_i}$, $s_i\mapsto T_i$ preserves all the relations of the Definition, and by the universal properties [F4] it defines an algebra homomorphism $\Phi\colon H_d\to\operatorname{End}_{\mathbb C}(\Omega)$. [F1, F4, algebra]

2.2 Triangular expansion. Fix $w\in S_d$ with a reduced word $w=s_{i_1}\cdots s_{i_k}$, and put $c:=\prod_{t=1}^k(\sigma_{i_1}\cdots\sigma_{i_{t-1}})(1-a_{i_t})\ne0$ in $\Omega$, with the empty prefix acting as the identity. Every transported factor is nonzero because the prefix is a field automorphism. In the expansion of $T_w=\prod_t\bigl((1-a_{i_t})\sigma_{i_t}-a_{i_t}\bigr)$ by the product rule of step 1.3, the term choosing the factor $(1-a_{i_t})\sigma_{i_t}$ for every $t$ contributes $c\,\sigma_w$ after the scalar coefficients are moved left, while every other term is $m_g\sigma_v$ with $v$ the product of a proper subword of $s_{i_1}\cdots s_{i_k}$ in the induced order. If $\ell$ denotes the minimal number of generators needed to express a permutation, then such a proper subword $J$ has $\ell(v)\le|J|<k=\ell(w)$, using subadditivity of $\ell$ and reducedness. Collecting the expansion in the $\Omega$-basis $\{\sigma_v\}$ therefore gives $T_w=c\,\sigma_w+\sum_{\ell(v)<\ell(w)}c_v\sigma_v$ with $c\ne0$ and $c_v\in\Omega$. [F1, step 1.3, algebra]

2.3 The evaluation homomorphism. The assignment $x_j\mapsto a+J_j$, $s_i\mapsto s_i$ defines an algebra homomorphism $\varphi\colon\mathcal F_d\to\mathbb C[S_d]$: the images of the $x$'s commute by step 1.5(i); the images of the $s_i$ satisfy the Coxeter relations by [F1]; and the cross relations follow from step 1.5(ii) and from $s_i(a+J_{i+1})=(a+J_i)s_i+1$, $(a+J_{i+1})s_i=s_i(a+J_i)+1$, which are step 1.5(iii) read in both directions. Since $\varphi(x_1-a)=a+J_1-a=0$, the quotient universal property [F4] yields an algebra homomorphism $\bar\varphi\colon H_d/(x_1-a)\to\mathbb C[S_d]$, which is surjective because the $s_i$ generate $S_d$. [F1, F2, F4, step 1.5, construct]

3.1 Independence of the monomials in the model. By step 2.2 the change-of-basis matrix from $\{T_w\}$ to $\{\sigma_w\}$ inside $D$ is triangular with nonzero diagonal when permutations are ordered by length, hence invertible over the field $\Omega$; thus $\{T_w:w\in S_d\}$ is an $\Omega$-basis of $D$. Suppose $\sum_{r,w}c_{r,w}m_{x^r}T_w=0$ in $D$ with $c_{r,w}\in\mathbb C$ finitely supported. Grouping by $w$ gives $\sum_wP_wT_w=0$ with $P_w=\sum_rc_{r,w}x^r\in\mathbb C[x_1,\dots,x_d]\subseteq\Omega$; $\Omega$-independence of the $T_w$ forces $P_w=0$ for every $w$, and linear independence of the monomials [F3] then forces $c_{r,w}=0$. Hence the elements $\Phi(x_1^{r_1}\cdots x_d^{r_d}w)$ are $\mathbb C$-linearly independent. [F3, step 1.3, step 2.2, algebra]

4.1 Basis theorem. Let $h\in H_d$ and write $h=\sum c_{r,w}x^rw$ using step 1.4. If $h=0$, applying the homomorphism $\Phi$ of step 2.1 gives $\sum c_{r,w}m_{x^r}T_w=0$, and step 3.1 yields $c_{r,w}=0$. Hence the ordered monomials form a $\mathbb C$-basis of $H_d$, and the $\mathbb C$-linear map $\mathbb C[x_1,\dots,x_d]\otimes_{\mathbb C}\mathbb C[S_d]\to H_d$, $f\otimes w\mapsto fw$, is an isomorphism by [F5]; in particular $\mathbb C[x_1,\dots,x_d]$ and $\mathbb C[S_d]$ are subalgebras of $H_d$ and the cross relations hold. The elementary cases $H_0=\mathbb C$, $H_1=\mathbb C[x_1]$ were recorded in step 1.1. [F2, F5, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 1.4]

5.1 The inverse map. In $H_d$ the relation $s_ix_{i+1}=x_is_i+1$ gives, after left multiplication by $s_i$ and use of $s_i^2=1$, the recursion $x_{i+1}=s_ix_is_i+s_i$. Hence in $H_d/(x_1-a)$ one has $x_1\equiv a$ and inductively $x_j\equiv a+u_j$ with $u_j$ in the subalgebra generated by the images of the $s_i$, namely $u_1=0$ and $u_{j+1}=s_ju_js_j+s_j$. By the basis theorem of step 4.1 every element of $H_d$ is a combination of monomials $x^rw$, and replacing each $x_j$ by $a+u_j$ expresses its image in $H_d/(x_1-a)$ as an element of the image of the subalgebra generated by the $s_i$; by [F1] and [F2] that image is the $\mathbb C$-span of $\{w:w\in S_d\}$. Therefore the canonical map $\rho\colon\mathbb C[S_d]\to H_d/(x_1-a)$, $w\mapsto w+(x_1-a)$, has image equal to the whole quotient, and it is injective because $\bar\varphi\circ\rho=\operatorname{id}_{\mathbb C[S_d]}$ by construction; hence $\rho$ is an isomorphism. Under it $x_j$ corresponds to $a+u_j$, and $\bar\varphi(a+u_j)=a+J_j$ by step 2.3, so $\bar\varphi(x_j)=a+\sum_{k<j}(k\ j)$; in particular $x_1$ corresponds to the scalar $a$, while for $j\ge2$ the image is not the scalar $a$. [F1, F2, step 4.1, step 2.3, algebra]

5.2 The degree filtration. For $k\ge0$ let $F_k\subseteq H_d$ be the image of the $\mathbb C$-span of all words in the symbols containing at most $k$ of the symbols $x_1,\dots,x_d$. Steps 1.4 and 4.1 identify $F_k$ with the span of the monomials $x^rw$ with $|r|\le k$. The substitution rules of step 1.4 replace an adjacent pair $s_ix_j$ by terms containing at most one $x$-symbol each, so a product of a word with $k$ $x$-symbols and a word with $m$ $x$-symbols rewrites into words with at most $k+m$ $x$-symbols; hence $F_kF_m\subseteq F_{k+m}$ and $(F_k)_{k\ge0}$ is an algebra filtration with $1\in F_0$. [F4, step 1.4, step 4.1]

6.1 The associated graded is a semidirect product. Let $S:=\mathbb C[x_1,\dots,x_d]\rtimes\mathbb C[S_d]$ be the algebra with $\mathbb C$-basis $x^rw$ and product $x^rw\cdot x^{r'}w'=x^{r+w\cdot r'}ww'$, where $(w\cdot r')_j=r'_{w^{-1}(j)}$; equivalently, $S$ is generated by the symbols $x_i$ and $w$ subject to the relations obtained from those of $H_d$ by deleting the inhomogeneous term $1$ from both cross relations, i.e. $s_ix_{i+1}=x_is_i$ and $x_{i+1}s_i=s_ix_i$. In $\mathrm{gr}\,H_d$ the defining relations of $H_d$ project to these relations: the commutativity, Coxeter and distant-commutation relations are homogeneous of the stated degrees, while the two cross relations have the form (degree $1$ element) $=1$ (degree $0$ element), so their degree-$1$ parts are exactly $s_ix_{i+1}=x_is_i$ and $x_{i+1}s_i=s_ix_i$. Consequently there is a surjective graded algebra homomorphism $S\to\mathrm{gr}\,H_d$ sending $x_i$ and $w$ to the symbols of $x_i$ and $w$. In degree $k$ both sides are $\mathbb C$-spanned by the symbols $x^rw$ with $|r|=k$: these form a spanning set of $\mathrm{gr}_kH_d$ by step 5.2 together with the basis theorem of step 4.1, and they form the basis of the degree-$k$ part of $S$ by construction; a surjection between $\mathbb C$-vector spaces with a spanning set of the same finite cardinality as a basis of the target is an isomorphism. Hence $\mathrm{gr}\,H_d\cong S$ in every degree, and the associated graded is the semidirect product $\mathbb C[x_1,\dots,x_d]\rtimes\mathbb C[S_d]$ in which $s_i$ swaps $x_i$ and $x_{i+1}$, as claimed. [F2, F5, step 4.1, step 5.2, algebra]

7.1 Polynomial grading boundaries. For $d=0$, step 1.1 gives $H_0=\mathbb C$ with its degree-zero grading; for $d=1$, it gives $H_1=\mathbb C[x_1]$ with the usual polynomial grading. For $d\ge2$, suppose there were an algebra grading $H_d=\bigoplus_{k\ge0}H_d^{(k)}$ with $x_i$ in degree $1$ and $s_i$ in degree $0$. Then the relation $s_ix_{i+1}-x_is_i=1$ would have its left-hand side in degree $1$ and its right-hand side in degree $0$, forcing $1=0$, which is impossible. Hence for $d\ge2$ the polynomial-degree filtration of step 5.2 does not arise from that generator grading; its cross relation is inhomogeneous. [F6, step 1.1, step 5.2] ∎

sections.heading: Remarks
sections.text:
- The filtration of step 4.1 is the polynomial-degree filtration, in which $x_i$ has degree $1$ and $s_i$ degree $0$ and the associated graded is commutative in the polynomial part but noncommutative overall; it is the filtration used for the cyclotomic quotients later on this page.

- The Arakawa-Suzuki generators $y_j$ used in the tensor constructions on this page are not the $x_j$ of this presentation: on a tensor module they differ by the scalar $z_M/N-(N-1)/2$ recalled in [[def-arakawa-suzuki-casimir-operators-on-tensor-functors]]. The presentation here is the one of [BKHL] and [BKAR]; both cross relations of the Definition are recorded because the recursion $x_{j+1}=s_jx_js_j+s_j$ used in step 3.3 consumes the second one.

- All arguments above are choice-free: the only selections made are finite (a monomial for the denominator clearing, a maximal permutation among finitely many), and no family of nonempty sets is used.

cases.specific_inspection: The affine Hecke Definition specifies a quotient of a free associative algebra and asserts its ordered-monomial basis and evaluation map; those constructive assertions are not a biconditional criterion.

The evaluation isomorphism sends polynomial generators to shifted Jucys–Murphy sums, with its inverse proved in Proof 5.1; it does not assert a converse characterization of arbitrary presented algebras.
The small ranks are admitted explicitly: Proof 1.1 and 7.1 give the scalar algebra in rank zero and the polynomial algebra in rank one, while higher ranks have an inhomogeneous cross relation.

The rational-function model uses a common denominator for finitely many coefficients and a maximal permutation in a finite symmetric group; the Remarks expressly describe these as finite selections without a choice principle.

sections.heading: Definition
sections.text:
Work in $\Lambda_{\mathbb Q}:=\mathbb Q\otimes_{\mathbb Z}\Lambda$, the
$\mathbb Q$-scalar extension of the stable graded ring
([[def-stable-graded-ring-of-symmetric-functions]]). Its power sums
$p_1,p_2,\dots$ ([[def-power-sum-and-complete-homogeneous-symmetric-polynomials]])
are algebraically independent generators:
$\Lambda_{\mathbb Q}=\mathbb Q[p_1,p_2,\dots]$, and for every $d$ the products
$p_\lambda$, $\lambda\vdash d$, form a $\mathbb Q$-basis of
$\Lambda_{\mathbb Q}^d$
([[prop-power-sums-form-a-rational-not-integral-stable-basis]]).

A **specialization** is a $\mathbb Q$-algebra homomorphism
$f\mapsto f[A]$ from $\Lambda_{\mathbb Q}$ to a commutative
$\mathbb Q$-algebra. By the algebraic independence of the power sums, a
specialization is determined by the sequence of values $\bigl(p_k[A]\bigr)_{k\ge1}$,
and conversely every sequence of elements of a commutative $\mathbb Q$-algebra
extends uniquely to a specialization. For specializations $A,B$, a scalar
$c\in\mathbb Q$ and a one-letter alphabet $t$ one defines the specializations
$A+B$, $-A$, $AB$, $c\cdot A$ and $tA$ by their power-sum values

$$p_k[A+B]:=p_k[A]+p_k[B],\qquad p_k[-A]:=-p_k[A],\qquad p_k[AB]:=p_k[A]\,p_k[B],$$

$$p_k[c\cdot A]:=c\,p_k[A],\qquad p_k[t]:=t^k\ \ \text{and hence}\ \ p_k[tA]=t^k p_k[A].$$

Here $c\cdot A$ is a coefficient multiplicity, to be distinguished from the
one-letter alphabet $t$, for which $p_k[t]=t^k$ is a power and
$p_k[tA]=t^k p_k[A]$; all occurrences of $tX$, $t^{-1}$, $tA$ and
$\sigma[t]$ on this page use this one-letter convention. The symbol $1$
denotes the one-letter alphabet with $p_k[1]=1$ for all $k$, and $-1$ denotes
its plethystic negative with $p_k[-1]=-1$ for all $k$
([[def-power-sum-and-complete-homogeneous-symmetric-polynomials]]); it is
**not** the ordinary one-letter alphabet whose letter is minus one, for which
$p_k$ would equal $(-1)^k$. One writes $f[A+B]$, $f[-A]$, $f[AB]$ and
$f[c\cdot A]$ for the images of $f$ under these specializations.

Define $X^{\perp}$ to be the specialization with $f[X^{\perp}]:=f^{\perp}$ for
all $f$, where $f^{\perp}$ is the adjoint of multiplication by $f$ with respect
to the Hall inner product $\langle\ ,\ \rangle_H$
([[def-hall-inner-product-on-symmetric-functions]]), characterized by
$\langle f^{\perp}g,h\rangle_H=\langle g,fh\rangle_H$. It exists and is unique
because the Hall form is nondegenerate on each finite-dimensional graded piece
$\Lambda_{\mathbb Q}^d$; the adjoints of commuting multiplication operators
commute, so the operators $f^{\perp}$ span a commutative
$\mathbb Q$-algebra and $X^{\perp}$ is a specialization in the sense above.

Define the series
$$\sigma[X]:=\sum_{n\ge0}h_n[X],$$
$h_n$ the complete homogeneous symmetric function
([[def-power-sum-and-complete-homogeneous-symmetric-polynomials]]).
Here $\sigma$ is interpreted in the graded completion of $\Lambda_{\mathbb Q}$
(or with a formal degree variable): it is a formal series, not an element of
$\Lambda_{\mathbb Q}$, and every occurrence of $\sigma$ below is to be read
degree by degree. Every Hall pairing of a series with a polynomial is the
finite sum obtained by truncating to the degrees of the polynomial. No
convergence of a scalar infinite sum is asserted, and no value of $\sigma$ at
a specialization with infinitely many letters is interpreted analytically.

cases.specific_inspection: A specialization is determined by its power-sum values and, conversely, every such sequence extends uniquely because the rational symmetric-function ring is a polynomial algebra; these are defining well-definedness clauses, not a separate reverse implication between theorem hypotheses.
