sections.heading: Statement
sections.text:
Fix any field $F$, level $\ell\ge1$, $q_H\in F^\times$ of finite order
$e\ge2$, charges $Q_a=q_H^{c_a}$, $n\ge0$, and the Lyle–Mathas parameters
$\mathcal O=F[t,t^{-1}]_{(t-1)}$, $z=q_Ht$, $U_a=Q_at^{na}$, with
$V=\nu_{t-1}\circ(-)$. Then for every multipartition shape $\lambda$ and
actual multipartition Schur weight $\nu$,
$$V(\det G_{\lambda\nu})=\sum_\mu J_{\lambda\mu}K_{\mu\nu},$$
where $K_{\mu\nu}$ is the semistandard Kostka number of
[[def-semistandard-tableau-and-kostka-number]] and $J_{\lambda\mu}=0$ unless
$\lambda$ strictly dominates $\mu$; otherwise $J_{\lambda\mu}$ is the sum over
all pairs of equal-length rim hooks removed from $\lambda$ and from $\mu$ to
the same remainder of $(-1)^{\operatorname{leg}_\lambda+\operatorname{leg}_\mu}$
times $V\bigl(\mathrm{res}_{\mathcal O}(\operatorname{foot}_\lambda)-\mathrm{res}_{\mathcal O}(\operatorname{foot}_\mu)\bigr)$,
the modulus $\nu_{t-1}$ of the Laurent difference of the two foot residues.
Every such difference is nonzero in $F(t)$. The full signed marked-strip
commutator and its auxiliary coefficient identity are proved locally below;
arbitrary-composition coefficients are combinatorial only and never introduce
extra Schur modules.

sections.heading: Facts & Assumptions
sections.text:
**Given:** The monic weight-Gram supplier [F1], the Laurent-binomial valuation
leaf [F2], the multipartition and Schur conventions [F3], the tableau
conventions [F4]–[F5], and the determinant convention [F6].

[F1] The exact monic product
$\det G_{\lambda\nu}=\prod_{T}\gamma_{t_T}/(C_{t_T}u_T)$ with the explicit
node-pair factors $C_+(A,B)=(zB-A)/(B-A)$ and
$R(A,B)=(zB-A)(B-zA)/(B-A)^2$
([[lem-cyclotomic-schur-weight-gram-determinants-are-products-of-monic-semistandard-norms]]).

[F2] For $k>0$, $V(z^k-1)=1$ in characteristic zero and $p^{v_p(k)}$ in
characteristic $p$, and $V$ is a valuation with $V(ab)=V(a)+V(b)$; the
valuation of a nonzero constant is $0$
([[lem-laurent-binomial-valuation-at-one-over-any-field]]).

[F3] Multipartitions, their dominance order, the flag condition and the
multipartition parameters $z,U_a$ over $\mathcal O$
([[def-arbitrary-level-cyclotomic-hecke-murphy-cell-and-schur-modules]]).

[F4] Standard tableaux, shapes, and contents
([[def-young-tableau-standard-tableau-and-shape]]).

[F5] Semistandard tableaux, weight, and the Kostka number
([[def-semistandard-tableau-and-kostka-number]]).

[F6] Determinants of square matrices over a commutative ring
([[def-determinant-of-a-square-matrix]]).

sections.heading: Proof
sections.text:
**Proof technique:** direct.

**Given:** The data and suppliers of [F1]–[F6]; work throughout with the fixed final-rank-$n$ parameters $z=q_Ht$, $U_a=Q_at^{na}$ at every auxiliary rank.

1.1 Characters as finite symmetric polynomials. Fix $d\ge n$ row labels per type component with ordered variables $x_{(a,r)}$, put $Y_a=\{x_{(b,r)}:b\ge a\}$ with the inherited order, and for a shape $\lambda$ let $\operatorname{ch}_\lambda(x)=\sum_{T\in\operatorname{SStd}(\lambda)}x^{\operatorname{wt}(T)}$. The flag condition says that the physical component $a$ of a semistandard tableau is an ordinary semistandard tableau over the alphabet $Y_a$, and the components are chosen independently, so $\operatorname{ch}_\lambda(x)=\prod_a s_{\lambda^{(a)}}(Y_a)$ with $s_\rho(Y)=\det(h_{\rho_i-i+j}(Y))$. The determinant equals the ordinary semistandard generating polynomial: expand it as signed families of east/north lattice paths from $(-j,1)$ to $(\rho_i-i,m)$ with east steps at height $r$ weighted $y_r$, choose the first intersection in a fixed order and exchange the two tails, an involution that preserves the monomial weight and reverses the permutation sign, so all intersecting families cancel; a nonintersecting family forces the identity matching, and the surviving families are exactly the semistandard tableaux, sign $+1$. Hence the coefficient of $x^\nu$ in $\operatorname{ch}_\lambda$ is the Kostka number $K_{\lambda\nu}$; empty and short-row cases are included. [F3, F4, F5, algebra]

2.1 Beta determinants and rim-hook signs. Choose $N\ge n$, put $\beta_{a,i}=\lambda^{(a)}_i+N-i$ with zero parts appended, and for a nonnegative integer array $v$ define $\chi(v;x)=\prod_a\det\bigl(h_{v_{a,i}-N+j}(Y_a)\bigr)_{i,j}$. If two entries of one component of $v$ agree the determinant has equal rows and is zero; otherwise sorting that component into strictly decreasing order and writing $\rho_i=v'_i-N+i$ gives $\chi(v;x)=\varepsilon(v)\prod_a s_{\rho^{(a)}}(Y_a)$ with $\varepsilon$ the product of the row-sorting signs, so every coefficient is a signed Kostka multiplicity. A beta move lowering a bead from $v+L$ to an unoccupied $v$ is exactly the removal of a rim hook of length $L$: tracing the southeast boundary shows the strip between the two boundary steps has $L$ boxes, its leg is the number of occupied positions strictly between $v$ and $v+L$, its foot content is $v-N+1$, and the associated sorting sign is $(-1)^{\operatorname{leg}}$; the correspondence is a bijection by the reverse move. [F4, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 The hook side as a complete finite alternating polynomial. Define $B_\lambda(x)$ as the finite alternating sum of step 2.1: for crosscomponent terms, over $a<b$, over beads $i,j$ and lengths $h\le\beta_{a,i}$, of $\chi(\beta-h e_{a,i}+h e_{b,j};x)V(U_az^{\beta_{a,i}-h}-U_bz^{\beta_{b,j}})$; and for same-component terms, over $a$, $i<j$ and $1\le h\le\beta_{a,i}-\beta_{a,j}-1$, of $\chi(\beta-he_{a,i}+he_{a,j};x)V(U_az^{\beta_{a,i}-h}-U_az^{\beta_{a,j}})$; terms whose $\chi$ is the zero polynomial are omitted before any valuation is evaluated. Then $B_\lambda(x)=\sum_{\mu:\lambda\triangleright\mu}J_{\lambda\mu}\operatorname{ch}_\mu(x)$: a crosscomponent move removing from the earlier component $a$ and adding to a later component $b>a$ produces a strictly dominated $\mu$ and occurs exactly once by the bead description; occupied targets give repeated rows and zero; sorting contributes $(-1)^{\text{removed leg}+\text{added leg}}$; and the prefactor $z^{-N+1}$ converts the beta difference to the difference of the deformed foot residues. In one component the two moved beads $i<j$ give a strict dominance decrease precisely for $1\le h<\beta_i-\beta_j$, the exchange case $h=\beta_i-\beta_j$ giving $\mu=\lambda$ and the outward case giving the reverse dominance; occupied intermediate positions again give zero rows, and the range exceeding a component's size gives a repeated or negative bead, hence a zero determinant. Thus no hook pair is lost or added, and the surviving summands are exactly the $J_{\lambda\mu}$ terms. [step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

3.2 Nonvanishing of every retained foot difference. For a removable rim hook of length $L$ from a partition of size $M+L$ with foot $(h,j)$, one has $-(M+L-1)\le j-h\le M$: every box left of the foot in its row survives, so $j-1\le M$, and $h\le M+L$ gives the lower bound. If $\lambda$ and $\mu$ remove equal-length hooks in distinct components $a\ne b$ to the same remainder with remainder sizes $M_a,M_b$, their foot contents satisfy $|\gamma_x-\gamma_y|\le M_a+M_b+L-1\le n-1$, so the exponent $n(a-b)+\gamma_x-\gamma_y$ is a nonzero integer; in the same component equal foot content and equal length reconstruct the same inverse hook addition, hence would force $\lambda=\mu$, which the strict-dominance terms exclude. Therefore every retained Laurent difference $U_az^u-U_bz^v$ is nonzero in $F(t)$: it is a unit times a nonzero Laurent monomial times $(z^{N}-1)$-type factors and, by [F2], its valuation is finite, being $0$ when the constant residues differ, $1$ in characteristic zero when they agree, and $p^{v_p(N)}$ in characteristic $p$ when they agree. [F2, step 2.1, algebra]

3.3 The same-component operator. In the same-component beta sum put $D=\beta_i-\beta_j$ and $k=D-h$, so the valuation is $f(k)=V(z^k-1)$ up to unit factors; swapping the two changed determinant rows shows $\chi(\beta-(D-k)e_i+(D-k)e_j;x)=-\chi(\beta-ke_i+ke_j;x)$. Hence the complete coefficient of $f(k)$ is $-\sum_{i<j:\beta_i-\beta_j>k}\chi(\beta-ke_i+ke_j;x)$, which is the strictly dominance-lowering part of $-p_kp_k^\perp$ on the abstract shape basis, where $p_k^\perp$ lowers an occupied bead by $k$ into an unoccupied nonnegative position with sign $(-1)^{\#\text{crossed beads}}$ and $p_k$ raises a bead by $k$ with the same sign rule; the bead-raising formula follows from the alternant identity $\det(y_r^{\beta_i})\sum_ry_r^k=\sum_i\det(y_r^{\beta_i+k\delta_{ij}})$ divided by the Vandermonde, and the removal map is its transpose. After one removal and one addition a non-diagonal lower-dominance result comes only from distinct beads $i<j$ with $0<k<\beta_i-\beta_j$, occupied intermediate positions giving zero repeated rows and the diagonal being removed by the strict projection; this proves the operator identification integrally, in every characteristic. [step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 The crosscomponent operator as exterior currents. On the $N$-fold exterior power of a space with basis $e_0,e_1,\dots$, represent a partition by the ordered wedge of its beta beads and let $E(p,q)$ insert $e_p$ after removing $e_q$, with exterior signs; it vanishes if $q$ is absent or $p$ is occupied, and its sign is the bead-sorting sign. Expanding $E=\text{creation}\cdot\text{contraction}$ gives $[E(p,q),E(r,s)]=\delta_{q,r}E(p,s)-\delta_{p,s}E(r,q)$. The crosscomponent matrix acting on column shape vectors is $J^{\mathrm{cross}}=\sum_{a<b}\sum_{h>0}\sum_{q\ge h,w\ge0}V(U_az^{q-h}-U_bz^w)E_a(q,q-h)E_b(w,w+h)$, a finite operator on each size-$n$ sector; the reverse hook pair has forward current $E_a(q-h,q)E_b(w+h,w)$, and transposing gives exactly this operator with the same signs and valuation. [step 3.1, step 3.2, step 3.3, algebra]

5.1 Horizontal strips and their conjugation. With $S e_q=e_{q+1}$ and $H(x)=(I-xS)^{-1}=\sum_{r\ge0}x^rS^r$, whose entry $H_{p,q}$ is $x^{p-q}$ for $p\ge q$ and $0$ otherwise, the matrix of $\wedge^NH(x)$ between $\beta_\mu$ and $\beta_\rho$ is $x^{|\mu|-|\rho|}\det(1_{\beta_{\mu,i}\ge\beta_{\rho,j}})$. Subtracting consecutive columns of the $0/1$ matrix makes its determinant $1$ exactly when $\beta_{\mu,i}\ge\beta_{\rho,i}>\beta_{\mu,i+1}$ for all $i$, i.e. $\mu_i\ge\rho_i\ge\mu_{i+1}$, the horizontal-strip criterion, and $0$ otherwise; so $\Gamma(x)=\wedge^NH(x)$ adds every horizontal strip once with weight $x^{\text{strip size}}$. For a type component $a$, $\Gamma_a(x)=\prod_{b\le a}\Gamma_b(x)$ adds a horizontal strip in every permitted physical component $b\le a$ and leaves the rest unchanged, so the successive $\Gamma_a$ from the empty shape enumerate exactly the flagged semistandard tableaux and give the branching matrix. Conjugation is explicit: since $H^{-1}=I-xS$ has column vector $e_p-xe_{p+1}$ and row covector $\sum_{r\le q}x^{q-r}e_r^*$, $\Gamma(x)^{-1}E(p,q)\Gamma(x)=\sum_{r=0}^qx^{q-r}\bigl(E(p,r)-xE(p+1,r)\bigr),$ and the two-current conjugation is the ordered product of two such sums. [step 4.1, algebra]

6.1 The marked-strip factor and the local commutator identity. For a permitted $\Gamma_a$ transition $\rho\to\lambda$ with new-node set $\eta$, put $r_x=U_{\operatorname{comp}(x)}z^{\operatorname{content}(x)}$ and $F^{(a)}_{\lambda\rho}=\prod_{x\in\eta}\prod_{\operatorname{comp}(x)<b\le a}(r_x-U_b)\prod_{\substack{x\in[\rho],\,y\in\eta\\x,y\ \text{same physical row}}}C_+(r_x,r_y)\prod_{\substack{x<y,\ x,y\in\eta\\\text{different physical rows}}}C_+(r_x,r_y)\prod_{\substack{x\in\eta,\,y\in[\rho]\\x<y}}R(r_x,r_y).$ Splitting the node pairs of [F1] into old/old, old/new and new/new pairs shows that along any semistandard chain the product of these factors is exactly $\gamma_{t_T}/(C_{t_T}u_T)$; older labels are smaller than the new label, same-row old/new pairs and same-label new/new pairs give $C_+$, a row-reading-earlier new node before an old node is a different-label inversion giving $R$, and all other pairs give nothing. Then $(J_n\Gamma_a^{(n,m)}-\Gamma_a^{(n,m)}J_m)_{\lambda\rho}=x^{n-m}V(F^{(a)}_{\lambda\rho})$ on permitted transitions and $0$ otherwise, on the reachable prefix sector. On support this is the exact row/column minor computation: the strip matrix is upper unitriangular, the row- and column-replacement determinants are $d_i^{\mathrm{row}}(v)=1_{p_i\le v<p_{i-1}}$ and $d_i^{\mathrm{col}}(v)=1_{q_{i+1}<v\le q_i}$ with $p_0=\infty$, the $J\Gamma$ term of index $j+1$ pairs with the $\Gamma J$ term of index $j$ sharing the bound $K_j=p_{b,j}-q_{b,j+1}-1$, and the elementary interval identity $\sum_{s=0}^{M-1}(\psi(A+s+K+1)-\psi(A+s+1))=\sum_{h=1}^{\min(M,K)}(\psi(A+M+K+1-h)-\psi(A+h))$ matches the two sides term by term, with $\psi(d)=V(U_az^d-U_b)$; the same-component telescoping is the analogue of this computation with the boundary factor. Off support, the defective strip step matrix has rank at most $N-2$, whence both sides vanish, or rank $N-1$ with one missing tail type $[P,P')$ and one duplicated type $(Q',Q]$; then the adjugate is $\varepsilon vu^{\mathsf T}$ with $u=e_i-e_{i+1}$, $v=e_r-e_{r-1}$ and one common sign, and replacing a row or column at position $x$ gives $D_{\mathrm{row}}(x)=\varepsilon u_l1_{P\le x<P'}$ and $D_{\mathrm{col}}(x)=\varepsilon v_l1_{Q'<x\le Q}$, so the a-only, b-only and both-defective cases cancel by the displayed interval translations; in the deficiency-two pattern with duplicate thresholds $r<s$ and missing intervals $I_1,I_2$ strictly between them, the row-side coefficient of $\phi(k)$ is $\varepsilon(A_{I_1}(k)B_{I_2}(k)-A_{I_2}(k)B_{I_1}(k))$ and the column-side coefficient is the same expression after the endpoint-reciprocity substitution $A_{I}=D^-$, $B_{I}=D^+$, so every formal coefficient cancels exactly, including adjacent missing thresholds and overlapping column groups, and higher deficiency kills both sides. [F1, F6, step 3.3, step 4.1, step 5.1, algebra]

7.1 Telescoping and the valuation formula. Multiply the $\Gamma$ matrices in increasing type-row-label order and telescope $J\Gamma-\Gamma J$ from $J_0=0$; by step 6.1 each commutator inserts exactly $V(F)$ at its strip position, so the $\lambda$-coordinate of the resulting identity is $\sum_{T}\gamma_{t_T}/(C_{t_T}u_T)=L_\lambda(x)$ on one side and $B_\lambda(x)$ on the other. All padded artificial symbols cancel before the surviving coefficients are evaluated, and every surviving coefficient corresponds to a valid current, hence by step 3.2 to a nonzero foot difference with finite valuation. Comparing with the exact monic product [F1] and the hook side of step 3.1, and taking the coefficient of $x^\nu$ at an actual multipartition weight $\nu$ (auxiliary compositions only index the same polynomials and never enter the Schur conclusion), gives $V(\det G_{\lambda\nu})=\sum_\mu J_{\lambda\mu}K_{\mu\nu};$ the empty case $n=0$ gives $0$, all ranks keep the fixed parameters $z=q_Ht$, $U_a=Q_at^{na}$, and arbitrary-composition coefficients are combinatorial only. [F1, step 3.1, step 3.2, step 6.1, algebra] ∎

sections.heading: Remarks
sections.text:
The lemma converts the exact monic determinant product of the sibling into
the signed rim-hook Kostka sum by an explicit exterior-current commutator and
a finite marked-strip case analysis; the foot-exponent bound makes every
retained valuation finite over any field, including the charged finite-order
regime. No choice principle is used: all sums, determinants, strips and
currents are finite.

cases.specific_inspection: The rim-hook valuation formula applies at every positive cyclotomic level through flagged alphabets and component factors; no separate single-level classification is stated.
The proof uses padded finite beta determinants, finite current sums on the fixed-rank sector and a fixed-order first-intersection involution on lattice paths; all combinatorial selections are finite.
The valuation Statement gives an equality between a determinant valuation and a signed rim-hook Kostka sum; Proof 7.1 obtains it by coefficient comparison, without a biconditional hypothesis.
The signed hook expression is a computed value, and the auxiliary composition coefficients are explicitly combinatorial; no converse producing Schur modules from those coefficients is claimed.
The valuation is algebraic at the prime generated by the deformation variable minus the unit; it is not an analytic endpoint limit, and all auxiliary ranks keep the same final-rank parameters.

Coincident constant foot residues are allowed in the charged finite-order regime: Proof 3.2 bounds the Laurent exponent away from zero and gives finite characteristic-dependent valuations when the constants agree.
Proof 7.1 expressly gives valuation zero in the empty rank; there the Gram determinant is the multiplicative unit and the signed current sum has no terms.
The rank hypothesis allows the empty multipartition and Proof 7.1 explicitly records its zero valuation; this matches the empty determinant convention imported from the monic Gram supplier.

sections.heading: Statement
sections.text:
(i) Let $K$ be a rational cohomological mixed Hodge complex
([[def-cohomological-mixed-hodge-complex]]). Then for every $n$ the vector
space $H^n(K_{\mathbb Q})$ carries a mixed Hodge structure whose weight
filtration is the shifted image filtration
$W_mH^n(K)=\operatorname{im}(H^n(W_{m-n}K)\to H^n(K))$ and whose Hodge
filtration is the image filtration
$F^pH^n(K_{\mathbb C})=\operatorname{im}(H^n(F^pK_{\mathbb C})\to H^n(K_{\mathbb C}))$.
In the weight spectral sequence $E_1^{p,q}=H^{p+q}(\operatorname{Gr}^W_{-p}K)$
one has $E_1^{p,q}$ pure of weight $q$, the sequence degenerates at $E_2$, and
$\operatorname{Gr}^W_mH^n(K)\cong E_2^{n-m,m}$ compatibly with the Hodge
filtrations. A morphism of cohomological mixed Hodge complexes induces, on
every $H^n$, a morphism of the resulting mixed Hodge structures.

(ii) Let $K^\bullet$ be a cosimplicial system of weight-zero rational Hodge
complexes concentrated in nonnegative cohomological degrees: cochain complexes
$K^{p,q}$ with coface maps and an internal differential satisfying the
cosimplicial identities, with $K^{p,q}=0$ unless $p,q\ge0$, whose differentials
are strict for the Hodge filtration, and with $H^q(K^p)$, together with the
induced $F$ and the rational comparison, a pure Hodge structure of weight $q$
for all $p,q$ (the axioms (GH1)-(GH2) of a cohomological Hodge complex of
weight zero). Form its simple
complex $sK$ with the standard total differential and the increasing filtration
$L$ by cosimplicial degree, $L_{-p}sK^n=\bigoplus_{i\ge p}K^{i,n-i}$. Then $sK$
is a rational cohomological mixed Hodge complex for the filtration $L$ and the
Hodge filtrations of the $K^p$, the cosimplicial spectral sequence
$E_1^{p,q}=H^q(K^p)\Rightarrow H^{p+q}(sK)$ degenerates at $E_2$, and
$\operatorname{Gr}^W_qH^n(sK)\cong E_2^{n-q,q}$; consequently all weights of
$H^n(sK)$ are at most $n$.

sections.heading: Facts & Assumptions
sections.text:
**Given:** A rational cohomological mixed Hodge complex $K$ with its axiom: for
every $w$, $\operatorname{Gr}^W_wK$ has finite-dimensional cohomology, its
differential is strict for the induced $F$, and $H^r(\operatorname{Gr}^W_wK)$
with its induced $F$ and rational comparison is a pure Hodge structure of
weight $r+w$ ([[def-cohomological-mixed-hodge-complex]]).

[F1] The cohomological filtered complex construction: for a cochain complex with a decreasing filtration by subcomplexes, degreewise finite, $E_1^{p,q}\cong H^{p+q}(\operatorname{gr}^pK)$ and the sequence naturally abuts to the decreasing image filtration with $E_\infty^{p,q}\cong\operatorname{gr}^pH^{p+q}(K)$; a filtered chain map induces compatible maps on all pages and on the abutments ([[thm-the-cohomological-filtered-complex-construction]]).

[F2] Morphisms of mixed Hodge structures are strict, their kernels, images and cokernels with induced or quotient filtrations are mixed Hodge structures, and a morphism from a structure of weights at least $q$ to one of weights at most $q'<q$ is zero: strictness gives $W_{q-1}$ of its image equal to zero and $W_{q'}$ of its image equal to the whole image, and $q'\le q-1$ forces the image to vanish ([[lem-morphisms-of-mixed-hodge-structures-are-strict]]).

[F3] A cochain complex has $d^{n+1}d^n=0$, so its differentials preserve every subcomplex filtration used below ([[def-cochain-complex-in-an-abelian-category]], [[def-cohomological-mixed-hodge-complex]]).

sections.heading: Proof
sections.text:
**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 (First page and pure strictness.) Put $G^p=W_{-p}$ and apply [F1] over $\mathbb Q$ and $\mathbb C$. Then $E_0^{p,q}=\operatorname{Gr}^p_GK^{p+q}$, $E_1^{p,q}=H^{p+q}(\operatorname{Gr}^W_{-p}K)$ and $E_\infty^{p,q}=\operatorname{Gr}^p_GH^{p+q}(K)$ for the image filtration. The axiom gives $E_1^{p,q}$ a pure rational Hodge structure of weight $q$. We will use the following explicit pure case of [F2]: a rational map preserving $F$ also preserves $\bar F$; between pure structures of the same weight it therefore preserves each type $F^a\cap\bar F^b$, so it is strict for $F$, and its kernels, images and cokernels have the induced pure structures. If the source has weight $q$ and the target has weight $q'<q$, it is zero: a source vector of type $(a,b)$ with $a+b=q$ maps into $F^a\cap\bar F^b$ of the target, which is zero because no target type of total $q'$ has both indices at least $a,b$. Thus no mixed Hodge structure on the abutment is being assumed. [F1, F2, given, algebra]

1.2 (Strict representative correction.) For a complex $C$ with decreasing filtration $T$ by subcomplexes and $T$-strict differential, the sequence $0\to H^n(T^aC)\to H^n(C)\to H^n(C/T^aC)\to0$ is exact for every $a,n$. For injectivity, a cycle $x\in T^aC$ that is a boundary $dy$ in $C$ equals $dy'$ for some $y'\in T^aC$ by strictness. For surjectivity, a quotient cycle lifts to $x\in C$ with $dx\in T^aC$; strictness gives $y\in T^aC$ with $dy=dx$, so $x-y$ is a cycle with the same quotient class. If a cycle maps to a quotient boundary, subtract a lift of that boundary to obtain a cycle in $T^aC$, proving exactness at the middle. In particular $H(T^aC)$ identifies with the filtration induced on $H(C)$ by $T^a$. These corrections use only strictness of the differential on $C$. [F3, construct, algebra]

2.1 (Exact filtered pages through $E_2$.) Fix a Hodge index $a$, and apply [F1] with the intersection and quotient $G$ filtrations to $A=F^aK_{\mathbb C}$, $B=K_{\mathbb C}$ and $C=B/A$. Their $E_0$ complexes form a short exact sequence $0\to E_0(A)\to E_0(B)\to E_0(C)\to0$: the first image in $G^pB/G^{p+1}B$ is $(F^aB\cap G^pB+G^{p+1}B)/G^{p+1}B$, exactly $F^aE_0(B)$, and the last term is its quotient. The mixed Hodge complex axiom says $d_0$ on $E_0(B)=\operatorname{Gr}^GK_{\mathbb C}$ is $F$-strict. Step 1.2 therefore gives a short exact sequence on $E_1$, with first image exactly $F^aE_1(B)$. Naturality of the page maps shows $d_1$ preserves this image for every $a$; its rational form then makes $d_1:E_1^{p,q}\to E_1^{p+1,q}$ a map of pure Hodge structures of weight $q$, strict by step 1.1. Apply step 1.2 again to the $E_1$ complexes to obtain exactness on $E_2$, with $E_2(A)$ identifying with the filtration induced on $E_2(B)=H(E_1(B),d_1)$. Denote this recursively induced filtration by $F_{\mathrm{rec}}$. The pure type decomposition of $E_1$ descends through its type-preserving $d_1$, so $E_2^{p,q}(B)$ with $F_{\mathrm{rec}}$ is pure of weight $q$. [F1, given, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 (Higher differentials and exact stable pages.) Suppose the three page complexes are exact at page $r\ge2$, with $E_r(A)$ identifying with $F^a_{\mathrm{rec}}E_r(B)$ for every $a$, and $E_r^{p,q}(B)$ pure of weight $q$. Naturality shows $d_r$ preserves these images, hence $F_{\mathrm{rec}}$; it also preserves the rational structures. Its target $E_r^{p+r,q-r+1}$ has lower weight, so step 1.1 forces $d_r=0$. This zero map is strict, and step 1.2 applied to the exact triple of $E_r$ complexes gives exactness at $E_{r+1}$ and the recursive filtration identification. Since $d_r(B)=0$, injectivity of $E_r(A)\to E_r(B)$ and surjectivity onto $E_r(C)$ also give $d_r(A)=d_r(C)=0$. Starting from step 2.1 proves this induction for all $r\ge2$. Thus the weight sequence degenerates at $E_2$, and the three sequences for $A,B,C$ stabilize there; $E_\infty^{p,q}(B)=E_2^{p,q}(B)$ is pure of weight $q$ for the recurrent filtration. [F1, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 (Recurrent filtration equals the abutment filtration.) By convergence and naturality [F1], the injective stable-page map $E_\infty(A)\to E_\infty(B)$ is $\operatorname{Gr}_G H(A)\to\operatorname{Gr}_G H(B)$ for the image $G$ filtrations on cohomology. A filtered linear map between finite filtered spaces whose graded map is injective is injective and strict: for any nonzero $x$, choose its largest decreasing-filtration index $p$; its nonzero graded class has nonzero image, so the image has this same index. This proves injectivity and, if the image of $x$ belongs to $G^p$, forces $x\in G^p$, which is strictness. The cohomology $G$ filtrations here are finite in each degree because $G$ is finite on the degree-$n$ cochain group, so the argument applies to $H^n(F^aK)\to H^n(K)$. Consequently its graded image is the induced filtration of the subspace $F^aH^n(K)=\operatorname{im}(H^n(F^aK)\to H^n(K))$ on $\operatorname{Gr}_GH^n(K)$: in filtration degree $p$ the numerator is $(F^aH^n(K)\cap G^pH^n(K))+G^{p+1}H^n(K)$. By steps 2.1 and 3.1 that same image on $E_\infty$ is $F^a_{\mathrm{rec}}$. This proves exactly the recurrent-to-abutment comparison needed here, with the strict representative correction supplied in step 1.2. [F1, step 1.2, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 (Mixed Hodge structure and shifted weights.) Write $W_mH^n(K)=\operatorname{im}(H^n(W_{m-n}K)\to H^n(K))$. Substitution $p=n-m$, $q=m$ in [F1] and step 3.1 gives $\operatorname{Gr}^W_mH^n(K)=\operatorname{Gr}^{n-m}_GH^n(K)\cong E_2^{n-m,m}$. Step 4.1 makes this identification compatible with the Hodge filtration induced by $F$ on cohomology; the right side is pure of weight $m$ by step 2.1. The rational comparison is an isomorphism on $E_1$ by the graded quasi-isomorphism axiom and hence on the stable pages; finite filtered leading-term descent makes it an isomorphism on cohomology as well. The finitely many nonzero stable terms in degree $n$ are finite-dimensional, so $H^n(K_{\mathbb Q})$ is finite-dimensional. The induced $W$ and $F$ are finite, and every $\operatorname{Gr}^W_m$ with its induced $F$ is pure of weight $m$, precisely the mixed Hodge axiom. [F1, given, step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, step 4.1, algebra]

6.1 (Functoriality.) A morphism of cohomological mixed Hodge complexes induces rational and complex cohomology maps compatible with the comparisons. It maps $W_{m-n}K$ to $W_{m-n}L$ and $F^aK_{\mathbb C}$ to $F^aL_{\mathbb C}$, hence preserves the cohomology image filtrations $W_m$ and $F^a$. These maps are therefore morphisms of the mixed Hodge structures of step 5.1. Naturality of [F1] and of the exact-page construction makes the graded-piece identifications compatible with these maps and their Hodge filtrations. [F1, given, step 4.1, step 5.1]

7.1 (The cosimplicial case.) Form $sK^n=\bigoplus_{p+q=n}K^{p,q}$ with the standard total differential. The cosimplicial identities, commutation with the internal differential and the usual total sign give $d^2=0$. The filtration $L_\ell sK^n=\bigoplus_{i\ge-\ell}K^{i,n-i}$ is increasing, by subcomplexes, and finite on each degree because $0\le i\le n$. Its graded piece is $\operatorname{Gr}^L_\ell sK\cong K^{-\ell}[\ell]$, so $H^r(\operatorname{Gr}^L_\ell sK)=H^{r+\ell}(K^{-\ell})$ is pure of weight $r+\ell$, and its internal differential is strict for $F$ by the Hodge complex hypothesis. Levelwise rational comparisons and filtration-preserving coface maps assemble to the total comparison, which is a graded quasi-isomorphism; the total complex is bounded below and its $F$ filtration is degreewise finite because each diagonal is finite. Thus $sK$ is a rational cohomological mixed Hodge complex for $L$. Applying steps 1.1-6.1 gives $E_1^{p,q}=H^{p+q}(\operatorname{Gr}^L_{-p}sK)=H^q(K^p)$, degeneration at $E_2$ and $\operatorname{Gr}^W_qH^n(sK)=\operatorname{Gr}^L_{q-n}H^n(sK)\cong E_2^{n-q,q}$, with its induced Hodge filtration and functorial mixed structure. Here $W_qH^n=L_{q-n}H^n$ is the shifted cohomology filtration, not the unshifted $L$. [F1, given, construct, step 1.1, step 3.1, step 5.1, step 6.1]

8.1 (Weights at most the degree.) Since the cosimplicial degree is nonnegative, $E_1^{p,q}=0$ for $p<0$, hence $E_2^{n-q,q}=0$ when $q>n$. Step 7.1 gives $\operatorname{Gr}^W_qH^n(sK)=0$ for all $q>n$; finiteness of the weight filtration then gives $W_nH^n(sK)=H^n(sK)$, proving the stated bound. [step 5.1, step 7.1, algebra] ∎

sections.heading: Source notes
sections.text:
Deligne III, Scholie (8.1.9), is the primary source for part (i). Deligne II
(1.3.15)-(1.3.17) supplies the comparison of direct, recurrent and abutment
filtrations used in its proof and in (3.2.5)-(3.2.10). Steps 1.2-4.1 instead
prove the comparison needed for this statement by exact spectral-sequence
pages for $F^aK\to K\to K/F^aK$, including the strict cycle and boundary
corrections; no unproved comparison is invoked. Theorem (8.1.15) and its proof
(8.1.17) are the source for the cosimplicial conclusion, whose weight-zero
special case is constructed in step 7.1. The shifted weight filtration is
kept distinct from the unshifted cosimplicial filtration. Weber (2.4.1) and
Arapura, Proposition 4.12 and Corollary 4.13, state the same cohomology
conclusion. Nothing above uses a choice principle or a splitting of a
filtration over $\mathbb Q$ or $\mathbb R$.

Part (ii) derives degeneration and the upper weight bound from a nonnegative cosimplicial system; no converse reconstructing such a system from a mixed Hodge structure is asserted.

sections.heading: Statement
sections.text:
Let $K$ be a finite geometric complex and $f:K\to\mathbb R^q$ piecewise smooth in
the sense of [[def-relative-smooth-triangulation-and-projection-preserving-fitting]].
There are subdivisions $K_m$ agreeing on every original face, with mesh
tending to zero and a single lower thickness bound $\theta>0$ for every
positive-dimensional simplex, whose secant maps $S_m$, defined by affine
interpolation of the values of $f$ at vertices, converge strongly in piecewise
$C^1$ to $f$.

If $L\subset K$ is a subcomplex and $U$ an open neighbourhood of $|L|$, the
approximation can instead be chosen pointwise equal to $f$ on a neighbourhood
of $|L|$ and equal to a secant map outside $U$, on shape-controlled
subdivisions; subdivision of $L$ is permitted and does not alter $f$ there, and
every affine target-plane constraint already satisfied by $f$ on original
simplices is preserved.

There is also a local extension statement: given a finite subcomplex
$A\subset K$, a sufficiently small strong approximation $g$ to $f|_A$ on any
subdivision extends to a prescribed small strong approximation $G$ to $f$ on a
subdivision of $K$, with $G=f$ and with the original simplices unchanged
outside the closed star of $A$. The permitted error of $g$ depends on the
requested error and the finite original simplices, not on the shape of the
subdivision of $A$. If the correction $g-f$ has zero component under an affine
linear target map $p$ on $A$, then the extended correction has zero $p$
component everywhere. This last extension does not assert a shape bound on its
coned simplices.

sections.heading: Facts & Assumptions
sections.text:
**Given:** the finite geometric complex $K$, the piecewise smooth map $f:K\to\mathbb R^q$, a subcomplex $L$ with an open neighbourhood $U$ of $|L|$, and a finite subcomplex $A$ with a strong approximation $g$ of $f|_A$ on a subdivision of $A$, in the sense of [[def-relative-smooth-triangulation-and-projection-preserving-fitting]].

[F1] Finite convex cell complexes admit compatible triangulations by coning from interior points, and barycentric subdivision has as vertices the face chains, so a chain all of whose barycentric vertices lie in a subcomplex lies in that subcomplex ([[lem-finite-convex-cell-complexes-admit-compatible-triangulations]], [[def-barycentric-subdivision-of-an-abstract-simplicial-complex]]).

[F2] Segment integration gives the value error of the linearization and chain-rule differentiation bounds composite corrections ([[cor-vector-valued-ftc-and-lipschitz-bound]], [[thm-chain-rule-for-total-derivatives]]).

[F3] Approximation and relative approximation have the meanings fixed in [[def-relative-smooth-triangulation-and-projection-preserving-fitting]]: strong $\delta$-approximation combines the value bound $\sup_b|g(b)-f(b)|<\delta$ with the derivative bound $|dg_b(v)-df_b(v)|<\delta|v|$ on every tangent-star vector, and shape control is a positive lower bound for $r(\sigma)/\operatorname{diam}\sigma$.

sections.heading: Proof
sections.text:
**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Lattice subdivisions with a uniform thickness bound. Give the finitely many vertices a total order and realize the abstract complex as a union of faces of one standard simplex $\Delta\subset\mathbb R^N$ with vertices $0,e_1,\dots,e_N$. The original geometric realization is related to this one by a linear isomorphism on each simplex, and finitely many such isomorphisms have uniformly bounded operator norms and inverse norms on their affine spans. In $\mathbb R^N$ cut the unit lattice cubes by the hyperplanes $\sum_i x_i=j$, $j\in\mathbb Z$, and all their faces; these cuts form a locally finite convex cell complex, since intersections arise by activating the shared supporting equalities. After translating a cube to $[0,1]^N$ only the cuts with $j=0,\dots,N$ occur, so there are finitely many cell shapes up to translation; triangulating every cell compatibly by [F1] with the translation-invariant choice of the average of its vertices gives finitely many simplex shapes, with maximal diameter $D$ and positive minimum thickness $\theta_0$ in positive dimensions. The simplex $m\Delta=\{x_i\ge0,\ \sum_i x_i\le m\}$ and each of its faces are unions of these cells, so scaling by $1/m$ gives subdivisions of $\Delta$, hence of the embedded abstract complex, with mesh at most $D/m$ and thickness at least $\theta_0$; restrictions to all faces agree because one global cell complex is used. Transporting back to the original realization multiplies diameter and inradius by the finitely many bounded factors of the linear isomorphisms, leaving the claimed mesh bound and one positive thickness $\theta$. Iterated barycentric subdivision has no such bound and is not used. [F1, algebra]

1.2 Combinatorial extension of a subdivision, and coned corrections. For the extension statement, extend the given subdivision of $A$ combinatorially in increasing dimension: keep every original simplex outside the closed star of $A$, and for each affected simplex whose boundary has already been subdivided, cone that boundary subdivision from the original barycentre. Each cone over a face simplex from the barycentre of the ambient simplex is a simplex, and the cones agree on common faces by the ray description of a simplex, so this produces a subdivision of $K$ containing the given subdivision of $A$. Suppose a correction $e=g-f$ is already defined and piecewise smooth on the subdivided boundary of an original simplex $\sigma$ with barycentre $c$; every $x\ne c$ in $\sigma$ has the unique expression $x=c+t(y-c)$ with $0<t\le1$ and $y\in\partial\sigma$. Choose a smooth scalar taper $a$ with $a(t)=0$ for $t\le1/3$ and $a(t)=1$ for $t\ge2/3$ and define $G(x)=f(x)+a(t)e(y)$ on $\sigma\setminus\{c\}$ and $G(c)=f(c)$. On each coned simplex this is smooth across $c$, because $a=0$ near $c$ forces $G=f$ there, and it assumes the prescribed values on the boundary; faces agree because $t$ and $y$ are determined by $x$ and $e$ is one function on the subdivided boundary. [F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 Secant estimate on a shape-controlled simplex. Let $s$ be a refined simplex inside an original simplex $\sigma$, with barycentre $b$, diameter $h$ and inradius $r\ge\theta h$, and put $T_b(x)=f(b)+Df(b)(x-b)$. On the compact simplex $\sigma$ the derivative of $f$ has a modulus of continuity $\omega_\sigma(h)\to0$ as $h\to0$, uniformly in the base point. Segment integration along $[b,x]$ gives $|f(x)-T_b(x)|\le h\,\omega_\sigma(h)$ for $x\in s$. The affine map $S_m-T_b$ interpolates the vertex errors $f(v)-T_b(v)$, each of modulus at most $h\,\omega_\sigma(h)$, and an affine function on a simplex attains its supremum at a vertex, so $\sup_s|S_m-T_b|\le h\,\omega_\sigma(h)$. For an affine map $A$ on $s$ with $\sup_s|A|\le E$ and a unit vector $v$ in the affine span of $s$, the point $b+rv$ lies in $s$ because $r$ is the inradius at the barycentre, so $|DA(v)|=|A(b+rv)-A(b)|/r\le2E/r$. Applying this to $S_m-T_b$ gives $\|DS_m-Df(b)\|\le2\omega_\sigma(h)/\theta$, and adding the continuity term $\|Df(b)-Df(x)\|\le\omega_\sigma(h)$ gives $\|DS_m-Df(x)\|\le(2/\theta+1)\omega_\sigma(h)$ for all $x\in s$. As the mesh tends to zero, both the value and the derivative errors tend to zero uniformly over all base points and all vectors of the refined tangent cones of $\sigma$; taking the maximum of the finitely many moduli $\omega_\sigma$ over the original simplices proves strong piecewise $C^1$ convergence. [F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 Extension error bounds. On a cone over a boundary simplex, $x=c+t(y-c)$; writing the barycentric coordinates of $x$ in $\sigma$ and summing those outside the face carrying $y$ shows that $t$ is an affine function of $x$ divided by the fixed barycentre-to-face height, and $y=c+(x-c)/t$. On the region $t\ge1/3$ the bounds $|Dt|\le C_1(\sigma)$ and $\|Dy\|\le C_2(\sigma)$ depend only on the original simplex, not on the subdivision of the boundary. The correction of step 1.2 has value $a(t)e(y)$ and derivative $a'(t)e(y)Dt+a(t)De(y)Dy$ by the chain rule, so its supremum norm and derivative norm are bounded by $C_\sigma\|e\|_{C^1}$ with $C_\sigma$ depending only on $\sigma$; near $c$ the correction vanishes identically. Hence, for finitely many affected simplices handled in increasing dimension, the product of the finitely many constants $C_\sigma$ converts any requested final error into a sufficient bound on the initial error, uniformly over all subdivisions of $A$; a zero correction on an already fixed subcomplex is retained, and the correction is zero outside the closed star of $A$ by construction. If $p$ is affine linear with $p(e)=0$ on $A$, then $p(a(t)e(y))=a(t)p(e(y))=0$, so a vanishing $p$ component is preserved. [F2, step 1.2, algebra]

3.1 Relative approximation with plane preservation. For the relative statement, barycentrically subdivide once if necessary so that $L$ is full: a face chain all of whose barycentric vertices lie in $L$ lies in $L$ by [F1]. Then let $d$ be the sum of the barycentric coordinates at vertices outside $L$; on each subdivision simplex the coordinates are affine, so $d$ is a global continuous piecewise affine nonnegative function, and its zero set is exactly $|L|$: a point of $|L|$ lies in a subdivision simplex all of whose vertices lie in $L$ because $L$ is full, so all coordinates outside $L$ vanish, while $d(x)=0$ forces $x$ into the hull of vertices lying in $L$, hence into $|L|$. The zero set of $d$ is closed and the complement of $U$ is compact, so the minimum of $d$ on $|K|\setminus U$ is a positive number $d_0$. Choose a smooth cutoff $\chi$ on $[0,\infty)$ with $\chi=0$ on $[0,d_0/3]$ and $\chi=1$ on $[2d_0/3,\infty)$ and values in $[0,1]$; its derivative is bounded, and the piecewise affine function $d$ has bounded derivative on the fixed finite subdivision. Setting $g_m=f+\chi(d)(S_m-f)$ gives, near $|L|$, $g_m=f$; outside $U$, $g_m=S_m$; and the derivative error is bounded by the derivative error of $S_m$ plus a fixed constant times its value error, both of which tend to zero by step 2.1. Each simplex restriction is smooth and face values agree. If $f$ maps an original simplex into an affine plane, then so do its vertex interpolants and every affine combination of $f$ with them, so all affine target-plane constraints are preserved, and the preliminary subdivision still admits the uniformly controlled subdivisions of step 1.1. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, step 2.1]

4.1 Assembly. The subdivisions of step 1.1 have mesh tending to zero and one positive thickness bound and, by step 2.1, their secant maps converge strongly in piecewise $C^1$ to $f$; step 3.1 provides the relative version, fixing $f$ near $L$, agreeing with a secant map outside $U$ and preserving affine target-plane constraints. For the extension statement, step 1.2 extends the subdivision and defines the coned correction, and step 2.2 bounds its $C^1$ norm by a constant depending only on the original simplices times the $C^1$ norm of the boundary correction, uniformly over all subdivisions of $A$; choosing the initial error small enough, in the finitely many affected simplices in increasing dimension, therefore realises any prescribed final strong-approximation error, keeps the correction zero outside the closed star of $A$, and preserves a vanishing affine-linear component. This proves all three assertions. [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1, step 2.2, step 3.1] ∎

sections.heading: Statement
sections.text:
Assume the Axiom of Choice, inherited from the published invariant-theory
items. Let $W$ act on the Cartan space $\mathfrak h$ by reflections and on
$S=S(\mathfrak h)$ by graded algebra automorphisms, with coinvariant algebra
$C=S/I$ as in [[def-the-coinvariant-algebra-of-a-finite-weyl-group]]. Then there
is a $W$-stable graded subspace $\mathcal H\subseteq S$, finite dimensional of
dimension $|W|$, such that the multiplication map
$$S^W\otimes_{\mathbb C}\mathcal H\longrightarrow S,\qquad p\otimes h\mapsto ph,$$
is an isomorphism of graded $S^W$-modules and of $W$-modules, and the
restriction of the quotient map $\rho:S\to C$ to $\mathcal H$ is an isomorphism
of graded $W$-modules $\mathcal H\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }C$. One may take
$$\mathcal H=\{f\in S:\partial_pf=0\text{ for all }p\in S^W_+\},$$
the kernel of the $W$-equivariant Laplacian attached to a $W$-invariant
positive definite form on $\mathfrak h_{\mathbb R}$, or any $W$-stable graded
complement of $I$. In particular $\dim\mathcal H_d=\dim C_d$ for every $d$ and
$\sum_d\dim\mathcal H_d=|W|$.

sections.heading: Facts & Assumptions
sections.text:
**Given:** A finite Weyl reflection group $W$ of rank $r$ acting on the real Cartan space $\mathfrak h_{\mathbb R}$ and on $S=\mathbb C[\mathfrak h]$ (page degrees, $\deg\mathfrak h=2$), its invariant algebra $S^W$, the ideal $I=S\,S^W_+$ with basic invariants $w_1,\dots,w_r$, and the coinvariant algebra $C=S/I$ with quotient map $\rho$.

[F1] Under AC, $S^W=\mathbb C[w_1,\dots,w_r]$ is a polynomial algebra on homogeneous basic invariants of page degrees $2d_i>0$, and $S$ is a free graded $S^W$-module of rank $|W|$ ([[thm-chevalley-shephard-todd-for-finite-weyl-groups]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]).

[F2] $I=S\,S^W_+$ is the ideal generated by the basic invariants, $C=S/I$ is a commutative graded $\mathbb C$-algebra with $C_0=\mathbb C$ generated in degree two, $\rho$ is surjective with kernel $I$, and $\operatorname{Hilb}(C,t)=\prod_i(1+t^2+\cdots+t^{2(d_i-1)})$, $\dim_{\mathbb C}C=\prod_id_i=|W|$; the $w_i$ are minimal homogeneous invariant generators, equivalently a homogeneous $S$-regular sequence realizing $I$ ([[def-the-coinvariant-algebra-of-a-finite-weyl-group]], [[lem-weyl-coinvariant-hilbert-series-has-order-w-dimension]], [[lem-reflection-basic-invariants-form-a-regular-sequence]]).

[F3] Every symmetric bilinear form on a finite-dimensional vector space has an orthogonal basis, and positivity is preserved under the constructions used below ([[def-bilinear-symmetric-skew-and-alternating-forms]], [[thm-symmetric-bilinear-forms-have-an-orthogonal-basis]]).

sections.heading: Proof
sections.text:
**Proof technique:** direct.

1.1 Choose an arbitrary positive definite symmetric bilinear form on $\mathfrak h_{\mathbb R}$ and average it over the finite group $W$, obtaining a $W$-invariant positive definite form $(\ ,\ )$; choose an orthonormal basis $e_1,\dots,e_r$ of $\mathfrak h_{\mathbb R}$ for it. On the symmetric algebra $S=\mathbb C[e_1,\dots,e_r]$ let $\langle\ ,\ \rangle$ be the Fischer pairing, the sesquilinear form with $\langle e^{\alpha},e^{\beta}\rangle=\alpha!\,\delta_{\alpha\beta}$ on monomials $e^{\alpha}$ ($\alpha$ a multi-index); it is positive definite, and $W$ acts on $S$ by orthogonal transformations for it because the form on $\mathfrak h_{\mathbb R}$ is $W$-invariant. For $p\in S$ let $\partial_p=p(\partial_1,\dots,\partial_r)$ be substitution of the partial derivatives $\partial_i=\partial/\partial e_i$; then multiplication by $p$ has adjoint $\partial_p$, i.e. $\langle pf,g\rangle=\langle f,\partial_pg\rangle$, as checked on monomials. Set $\mathcal H_d:=I_d^{\perp}$ inside the finite-dimensional space $S_d$, and $\mathcal H:=\bigoplus_d\mathcal H_d$. [F3, construct]

1.2 The invariant ring acts on $S$ with the expected Hilbert series: $S$ has a finite homogeneous $S^W$-basis by [F1], say of degrees $m_1,\dots,m_{|W|}$; their images in $S/S^W_+S=C$ form a $\mathbb C$-basis by graded Nakayama, so $\sum_jt^{m_j}=\operatorname{Hilb}(C,t)$ and therefore $\operatorname{Hilb}(S,t)=\operatorname{Hilb}(S^W,t)\operatorname{Hilb}(C,t)$. [F1, F2, algebra]

2.1 By step 1.1 the spaces $S_d=I_d\oplus\mathcal H_d$ are orthogonal direct sums and $\mathcal H$ is a graded subspace; it is $W$-stable because $W$ preserves the form and $I$ is a $W$-stable homogeneous ideal, and $\mathcal H$ is a graded complement of $I$. Moreover $\mathcal H_d=\{f\in S_d:\partial_pf=0\text{ for all }p\in S^W_+\}$: since $I=(w_1,\dots,w_r)$, one has $f\in I_d^{\perp}$ exactly when $\langle f,w_ig\rangle=0$ for every $i$ and every $g\in S_{d-2d_i}$, which by adjointness is $\langle\partial_{w_i}f,g\rangle=0$ for all such $g$, hence $\partial_{w_i}f=0$ by positive definiteness; and for $p=\sum_iq_iw_i$ one has $\partial_p=\sum_iq_i\partial_{w_i}$, so vanishing for the $w_i$ is vanishing for all of $S^W_+$. [step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 The restriction $\rho|_{\mathcal H}:\mathcal H\to C$ is an isomorphism of graded vector spaces because $\rho$ has kernel $I$ and $\mathcal H$ is a complement of $I$ by step 1.1; it is a map of $W$-modules because $\rho$ is $W$-equivariant. Hence $\dim\mathcal H_d=\dim C_d$ for every $d$, and $\dim\mathcal H=\dim C=|W|$ by [F2]. [F2, step 1.1]

3.1 Let $\varphi:S^W\otimes\mathcal H\to S$, $p\otimes h\mapsto ph$. This is a homomorphism of graded $S^W$-modules and of $W$-modules. Its reduction modulo $S^W_+$, namely $C\otimes\mathcal H\to C$, $c\otimes h\mapsto c\,\rho(h)$, is surjective because it restricts on $1\otimes\mathcal H$ to the isomorphism $\rho|_{\mathcal H}$ of step 2.2. [step 2.1, step 2.2]

4.1 The map $\varphi$ is surjective: given homogeneous $f\in S_d$, choose $h\in\mathcal H_d$ with $\rho(f)=\rho(h)$ by step 3.1; then $f-h\in I_d=\sum_i(w_iS)_d=\sum_iw_iS_{d-2d_i}$, so by induction on $d$ each $w_ig$ with $g\in S_{d-2d_i}$ lies in $S^W\cdot\mathcal H$, and adding $h$ exhibits $f$ in the image. [step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra]

5.1 The map $\varphi$ is injective: by steps 1.2 and 2.2 the two sides have the same Hilbert series, $$\operatorname{Hilb}(S^W\otimes\mathcal H,t)=\operatorname{Hilb}(S^W,t)\operatorname{Hilb}(\mathcal H,t)=\operatorname{Hilb}(S^W,t)\operatorname{Hilb}(C,t)=\operatorname{Hilb}(S,t),$$ both are graded with finite-dimensional graded pieces, and by step 4.1 the kernel of the surjective graded $S^W$-linear map $\varphi$ would otherwise contribute positive Hilbert series. Hence $\varphi$ is an isomorphism. [step 1.2, step 2.2, step 4.1, algebra]

6.1 Steps 2.1, 2.2 and 5.1 give a $W$-stable graded complement $\mathcal H$ of $I$ with $\rho|_{\mathcal H}:\mathcal H\cong C$ and $S^W\otimes\mathcal H\cong S$; the description of $\mathcal H$ as the kernel of the Laplacian follows from the adjointness $\langle pf,g\rangle=\langle f,\partial_pg\rangle$ of step 1.1, and $\dim\mathcal H=|W|$ by step 2.2. The Axiom of Choice is inherited from the invariant-theory suppliers [F1] and [F2]; the construction itself uses only finite averages and finite-dimensional linear algebra. [F1, F2, step 2.1, step 2.2, step 5.1] ∎

cases.specific_inspection: The harmonic Statement constructs a graded Weyl-stable complement and its multiplication and quotient isomorphisms; Proof 2.2 and 5.1 establish those maps rather than an equivalence of predicates.
The allowed complements provide models of the coinvariant representation; the Statement does not claim a converse recovering the Weyl action or invariant ring from an arbitrary complement.

In rank one the Fischer pairing and the ideal generated by one basic invariant still give the degreewise orthogonal complement of Proof 1.1; the quotient and equal-Hilbert-series argument uses the same finite graded pieces.
